127.name: Place value
127.description: In this unit pupils revisit, secure and develop their understanding of place value with integers, decimals, fractions, metric and imperial units. This knowledge is then extended to order and compare numbers of increasing complexity.
127.why: We begin year 7 with checking, securing and further development of place value in order to prepare adequately for further work on number in the following units for this term.
prior: Understand value of digits in large and decimal numbers
Multiply and divide by powers of 10
Convert between standard and decimal forms

64.name: Properties of number: factors, multiples, squares and cubes
64.description: In this unit pupils develop their understanding of factors and multiples, then extend this knowledge to learn general divisibility tests for integers and develop strategies to determine the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of two or more integers.
64.why: This unit continues to develop proficiency in handling and recognising different types of numbers, as well as understanding their mathematical structure in order to be more efficient and fluent with mathematical operations in the following unit.
prior: Identify and list factors and multiples
Recognise and calculate square and cube numbers
Apply divisibility rules and prime factorisation

87.name: Arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals
87.description: In this unit pupils develop their ability and efficacy with the four operations including more complicated and challenging calculations involving fractions, decimals and negative numbers. This leads into an exploration of the priority order of operations.
87.why: This unit builds on knowledge established in work on factors, multiples squares and cubes, building on the understanding that any positive integer can be expressed as a product of its factors. This skill is used here to explore multiplying and dividing with decimals.
prior: Perform all four operations with whole numbers
Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals
Apply integer rules (positive/negative) to calculations

160.name: Expressions and equations
160.description: In this unit, pupils learn about generalisation and formal algebraic manipulation techniques such as substitution, collecting like terms and factorising.
160.why: This unit is a natural extension of the number work in the previous units. We are now seeking to generalise patterns and behaviours that were first seen in the number units taught before, and pulling in key skills such as factorisation and multiplication of brackets as part of algebraic manipulation.
prior: Simplify algebraic expressions
Solve linear equations and substitute values
Rearrange and manipulate formulas

191.name: Plotting coordinates
191.description: In this unit pupils revisit and further develop their understanding of the coordinate plane, and learn how to plot non-integer coordinates. Pupils then plot from an equation both by hand and by using technology.
191.why: Continuing from their recent work using algebra, this unit introduces plotting from algebraic equations and developing generalisations from a set of coordinate pairs.
prior: Understand and use axes in all four quadrants
Plot and read coordinates accurately
Recognise and describe geometric figures using coordinates

217.name: Perimeter and area
217.description: In this unit pupils investigate how to calculate the area and perimeter of rectilinear shapes, and composite shapes using rectangles and triangles. They will also derive simple area formulae.
217.why: This unit requires some confidence in the use of formulae and simple algebra, hence it has been positioned after pupils have done some work on algebraic manipulation and number operations. This unit also prepares pupils for further work on geometry later in the year.
prior: Identify 2D shapes and their properties
Use and apply standard formulas for area and perimeter
Calculate with units of length and area

273.name: Comparing and ordering fractions and decimals (positive and negative)
273.description: This unit develops understanding and manipulation of fractions, including conversion between fractions to terminating and recurring decimals. Pupils then learn strategies to order fractions of increasing complexity.
273.why: This unit builds upon work done in the 'arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals' unit, supporting further development of fluency in working with decimals as well as fractions.
prior: Recognise and convert between fractions and decimals
Understand number lines with negative values
Compare values using place value and visual representations

326.name: Arithmetic procedures with fractions
326.description: This unit revisits and secures fraction operations and extends pupil understanding to division of whole numbers by fractions and division of fractions by fractions.
326.why: This unit continues from the previous one in deepening pupil understanding of fractions whilst also being explicitly linked to the 'arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals' unit.
prior: Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions
Simplify fractions and find common denominators
Convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers

331.name: Understanding multiplicative relationships: fractions and ratio
331.description: This unit introduces the concept of multiplicative relationsihps, and connects fractions to the idea of ratios. Ratios are then explored in depth and used to solve contextual problems such as those involving exchange rates and general conversions.
331.why: This unit finishes our work with fractions in Year 7, relying upon pupil understanding of multiplication of fractions, and explicitly connecting fractions with ratios and general multiplicative relationships.
prior: Convert between fractions and decimals
Use fractions to represent parts of a whole
Apply ratios to compare and scale quantities

341.name: Transformations
341.description: This unit introduces pupils to shape tranformations: enlargements, rotations, reflections and translations both by hand and with technology.
341.why: This unit utilises prior knowledge with ratios and percentages, applying general multiplicative relationships to the transformation of shapes, whilst also drawing upon recently developed knowledge of the coordinate plane.
prior: Identify and describe reflections, rotations, translations and enlargements
Plot points and shapes in all four quadrants
Use coordinates to represent movements

350.name: Estimation and rounding
350.description: This unit helps pupils understand rounding to different decimal places, and significant figures. Pupils will also learn how to truncate numbers and understand the contexts in which these skills are useful. The unit ends will an exploration of rounding and inequality errors.
350.why: Students up to this point have been working with integer values and have had few opportunities to work explicitly on estimation. We are starting the year with something that is familiar for students and extend knowledge of estimation and rounding to include more work on rounding with decimals and significant figures.
prior: Round numbers to nearest 10, 100, 1000
Round decimals to 1 or 2 decimal places
Estimate calculations using compatible numbers

361.name: Sequences
361.description: In this unit we develop knowledge of sequences to be able to identify, determine, and continue arithmetic sequences. We finish the unit by looking at how sequences may be reprsented graphically.
361.why: In this unit pupils are developing their knowledge of plotting coordinates by exploring the idea that a set of points can satisfy a mathematical relationship. This unit sets the foundation for working with graphical representations of linear equations.
prior: Recognise and continue number patterns
Understand position-to-term rules
Use nth term to generate a sequence

372.name: Graphical representations of linear equations
372.description: In this unti we develop understanding of linear relationships and explore the key features of a linear equation such as the gradient, intercept and determining an equation from coordinate pairs.
372.why: In this unit we continue to build on knowledge developed in the previous work on sequences and build confidence in how a linear sequence produces a linear relationship. We represent that graphically along with development of understanding of the equation of a line, positive, negative relationships and the idea that a linear sequence can produce an infinite set of points.
prior: Rearrange equations into y = mx + c form
Use tables of values to plot lines
Identify features of straight-line graphs

375.name: Solving linear equations
375.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to find a value that satisfies a linear relationship when one value is known both with a single step operation, and multiple step operations. A variety of cases are explored including using brackets and rearranging.
375.why: Further to graphing linear sequences in the previous unit, pupils now learn to connect understanding with solving linear equations after demonstrating how for each point on a linear graph there is a unique solution to the equation of the line.
prior: Understand and apply inverse operations
Simplify algebraic expressions
Solve one-step and two-step equations

384.name: Understanding multiplicative relationships: percentages and proportionality
384.description: In this unit pupils explore multiplicative relationships with percentages, direct and inverse proportion.
384.why: Pupils build upon key stage 2 work with finding percentages of amounts, then extending their knowledge to percentage change, connecting to previous learning around decimals and fractions. Pupils then explore a more general exploration of multiplicative relationships.
prior: Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages
Understand ratio and scaling
Solve problems involving direct proportion

395.name: Graphical representations of data
395.description: In this unit pupils will interpret and construct a range of representations of data including bar charts, pie charts and scatter graphs.
395.why: Pupils have prepared for this unit earlier in the year by looking at graphical representations of sequences. We build upon that knowledge to show that data can be represented in further ways as well as how to construct and interpret those representations.
prior: Draw and interpret bar charts, line graphs and pie charts
Choose appropriate graphs for different types of data
Understand and use frequency and grouped data

406.name: Numerical summaries of data
406.description: In this unit pupils explore the concept of measures of central tendancy, developing understanding of different types of average and their relative benefits and drawbacks. We then investigate other summaries of data such as the range and data comparison techniques.
406.why: Building on work pupils have undertaken on averages in key stage 2, and linking to the previous unit where we summarised data graphically, pupils now explore representing data numerically. Pupils focus on the concept of measures of central tendency and range. We also begin to look at correlation as a relationship between data.
prior: Calculate mean, median, mode and range
Organise data in frequency tables
Interpret results in context

417.name: Perimeter, area and volume
417.description: In this unit pupils extend their knowledge of shapes by exploring the properties of circles and composite shapes before developing understanding of 3-D shapes including surface area and volume.
417.why: This unit is an extension of the perimeter and area unit in year 7 (which focused on polygons), and extends this knowledge to focus on circles and circle based composite shapes then extending to look at the concept of prisms and volume.
prior: Use standard formulas for rectangles and cuboids
Convert between units of measure
Calculate dimensions of composite shapes

428.name: Geometrical properties: polygons
428.description: In this unit pupils will investigate internal and external angles of polygons and angles made with a transveral and parallel lines. Pupils will develop their ability to formally prove properties of polygons to generalise.
428.why: This unit builds on knowledge developed investigating angles and continues work done in the previous unit investigating polygons. Here pupils will develop understanding of external and internal angles of polygons and traversals through parallel lines
prior: Identify and classify polygons by sides and angles
Use angle rules (interior, exterior)
Calculate sum of angles and solve problems using reasoning

439.name: Constructions
439.description: In this unit we develop skills in using a pair of compasses and ruler to construct various accurate shapes and angles including triangles, rhombi, perpendicular lines and angle bisectors.
439.why: After studying polygons and circles in depth in previous units, this year culminates in learning to mathematically construct these shapes using knowledge of the properties of triangles, quadrilaterals and circles in order to draw them accurately.
prior: Use ruler and compass for straight-edge and arcs
Construct perpendiculars and bisectors
Interpret geometric conditions in drawings

449.name: Geometrical properties: similarity and Pythagoras' theorem
449.description: This unit explores the concepts of congruence and similarity, and ways to prove or disprove similarity between shapes. We then explore further properties of triangles with Pythagoras' Theorem.
449.why: This unit builds on knowledge developed in work on transformations, angles and properties of triangles. Pupils explored the effects of different transformations and whether the transformed shape was congruent or similar to the original shape. This knowledge is built upon and applied to new contexts as pupils formalise the criteria for determining congruence in triangles and study rotational symmetry. This unit also prepares pupils for learning about trigonometry to extend a right-angled triangle in the unit circle to any other right-angled triangle.
prior: Recognise right-angled triangles
Apply Pythagoras' Theorem to find missing lengths
Use ratios in similar shapes

459.name: Probability: possible outcomes
459.description: This unit introduces and explores the concept of liklihood as a relative measure, and demonstrates multiple ways to represent likelihood such as Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and two-way tables.
459.why: This unit is the first introduction to probability and likelihood. Pupils develop their understanding of how likely something is, looking at relative likelihoods and displaying outcomes but without formalising probability using measurable numerical values at this stage. Pupils explore different ways to display outcomes to gain a sense of what it means to say something is likely or unlikely in preparation for more calculative methods and theoretical probability in the next unit.
prior: Understand outcomes and sample spaces
Use fractions and percentages to represent probability
Recognise equally likely events and basic probability rules

513.name: Probability: theoretical probabilities
513.description: In this unit we build upon the concept of likelihood to work more mathematically with more measurable probability using fraction and decimal representations to both interpret and calculate. We revisit and develop ways to represent and compare probabilities.
513.why: Further to developing the basic ideas and foundations of probability, we move towards more abstract measures of likelihood using calculations to assign numerical values to probability. We then revisit the visual models of probability established in the previous unit through the lens of representing and utilising theoretical probability.
prior: Define probability as a ratio between favourable and possible outcomes
Represent events using lists, tables or diagrams
Calculate probabilities of single and combined events

602.name: Non-linear relationships
602.description: In this unit we explore geometric and special number sequences like the Fibonacci sequence. We develop strategies to recognise types of sequence and continue them.
602.why: This unit builds from the sequences unit in Year 8. We develop understanding of sequences further to look at geometric and other non-linear sequences and how they appear graphically.
prior: Recognise non-linear patterns in graphs and tables
Understand simple quadratic and exponential relationships
Plot and interpret curves on coordinate grids

626.name: Expressions and formulae
626.description: This unit develops pupil understanding of formulae and how to rearrange them. Pupils will learn how to recognise and manipulate binomials and learn to recognise the difference of two squares.
626.why: This unit builds on solving linear equations from year 7 where pupils learnt to rearrange aan equation to find a specific value that satisfied the equation. In expressions and formulae, pupils use their understanding of rearrangement to change the subject of a formula. Pupils are then introduced binomial equations in preparation for trigonometry.
prior: Simplify algebraic expressions
Use substitution in expressions and formulas
Rearrange formulas involving one or more steps

707.name: Trigonometry
707.description: In this unit pupils learn how to recognise the relationship between the unit circle and the trigonometric ratios of sine, cosine and tangent. Pupils then apply this knowledge to solve trigonometric problems.
707.why: Pupils have recently learned about geometrical properties of similarity and the Pythagorean Theorem. This knowledge is further developed to build on their understanding of congruence and similarity with right-angled triangles. In this unit, similarity is used to extend a right-angled triangle in the unit circle to any other right-angled triangle.
prior: Label sides in right-angled triangles (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse)
Use sine, cosine and tangent ratios
Rearrange and solve trigonometric equations

787.name: Standard form
787.description: In this unit pupils learn to recognise, interpret and write in standard form. Pupils then extend this knowledge so that they can order numbers written in standard form.
787.why: This unit builds from arithmetic procedures with integers and decimals. In the prior unit, pupils learnt how to factorise multiples of 10 in order to simplify calculations. This understanding is further developed in this unit as values are converted to meet the conditions for standard form.
prior: Understand place value and powers of 10
Convert between standard and ordinary notation
Multiply and divide using powers of 10

862.name: Graphical representations
862.description: In this unit pupils draw, interpret and utilise linear graphs to solve problems. This knowledge is further extended to look at intersecting graphs.
862.why: This unit builds knowledge from previous work on non-linear relationships. In that unit, pupils considered geometric sequences and how they might be represented graphically. In this unit, pupils study the graphical representation to link features of the graph to its equation.
prior: Plot points and draw axes
Interpret bar charts, line graphs, and scatter graphs
Select appropriate graphs for different types of data

450.name: Maths and the environment
prior: Interpret real-world contexts using mathematical reasoning
Use units and conversions appropriately
Read and represent data using graphs and tables

451.name: Maths in the workplace
prior: Read tables, charts, and schedules
Perform calculations with money and units
Interpret job-based and practical contexts using maths

452.name: Thinking critically with maths
prior: Interpret and evaluate information logically
Justify reasoning using numerical and graphical evidence
Identify assumptions and question validity of arguments

1719.name: Calculator functionality
1719.description: This unit teaches how to use scientific calculators and expores their functionality
1719.why: It is important to dedicate some time to understanding the functionality of modern scientific calculators so that they can be used appropriately.
prior: Perform basic operations accurately
Use brackets, powers, roots and memory functions
Interpret calculator display and rounding appropriately

1976.name: Algebraic manipulation
1976.description: In algebraic manipulation, pupils use apply knowledge of the distributive law to find the product of two binomaials in order to factorise quadratics.
1976.why: This unit is the foundation for a lot of the generalisation done in this year, and is placed at the start of the year accordingly.
prior: Collect like terms and use basic algebra
Expand and factorise expressions
Substitute values into algebraic formulas

1980.name: Simultaneous equations: 2 variables
1980.description: In this unit pupils will learn to solve a pair of simultaneous equations from different starting points and cases using a variety of strategies.
1980.why: This unit builds from solving equations in Year 8 and develops those skills further.
prior: Solve linear equations in one variable
Interpret solutions graphically
Substitute values into expressions

1982.name: Percentages
1982.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to perform simple and compound interest calculations using percentages.
1982.why: This unit builds from percentage change and because it utilises a formula it follows on from more work on algebra.
prior: Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages
Find percentages of amounts (including 50%, 25%, 10%)
Use percentage increase/decrease in context

1984.name: Arithmetic procedures: index laws
1984.description: In this unit pupils learn how to manipulate indices and perform calculations without conversion by understanding index laws.
1984.why: This unit builds on the index work covered in the previous unit to formalise laws around indices.
prior: Understand and apply powers and roots
Use rules for multiplying and dividing powers
Apply zero, negative and fractional indices

1190.name: Standard form calculations
1190.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers written in standard form.
1190.why: This unit deepens pupil understanding of index laws to now cover standard form.
prior: Understand powers of 10 and place value
Convert numbers to and from standard form
Perform calculations using multiplication/division of powers of 10

1978.name: Surds
1978.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to recognise surds, handle them in calculations and rationalise fractions with surds as denominators.
1978.why: This unit continues to build knowledge around the use of indices, looking deeper at fractional indices and surds in general.
prior: Understand square and square root notation
Simplify square roots of integers
Multiply and divide simple surds

1881.name: Sampling
1881.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to sample, and explore accuracy and limitations with various sampling strategies and data collection techniques.
1881.why: This topic is placed here to benefit from interleaving and builds from prior learning around numerical summaries of data.
prior: Understand the concept of a population and sample
Recognise bias and representativeness
Select and justify methods of sampling

1317.name: Graphical representations of data: scatter graphs and time series
1317.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to interpret and extract data from scatter graphs and time series graphs.
1317.why: This unit builds from data sampling to deepen understanding of the ways in which data can be interpreted and interrogated.
prior: Plot coordinates in all four quadrants
Interpret trends and patterns in data
Understand correlation and basic statistical language

1883.name: Comparisons of numerical summaries of data
1883.description: In this unit pupils will compare two different data sets and compare different measures of central tendancy when interpreting the data. Pupils will learn to interrogate frequency tables and stem and leaf diagrams both with and without technology.
1883.why: This unit benefits from the preceding units on data collection and representations. It furthers pupil understanding of data representation and interrogation.
prior: Calculate mean, median, mode, and range
Interpret and compare sets of data
Understand the purpose of each statistical measure

1987.name: Rounding, estimation and bounds
1987.description: This unit explores the impact of upper and lower bounds on additive and multiplicative calculations.
1987.why: This unit builds upon ideas around data accuracy and projection that are covered in prior data units this year.
prior: Round whole numbers and decimals appropriately
Estimate answers using compatible numbers
Understand upper and lower bounds in calculations

1989.name: Ratio
1989.description: In this unit pupils will learn how to combine ratios, interpret algebraic ratios, and investigate quantity changes and their effect on ratios.
1989.why: This unit builds on prior knowledge of simple ratios but deepens understanding by moving into new areas of practical application and generalisation..
prior: Use language of ratio and proportion
Divide quantities in a given ratio
Scale values up or down using ratios

1991.name: Linear graphs
1991.description: In this unit pupils consider equations that produce parallel or perpendicular graphs and how their equations relate to each other.
1991.why: This unit requires strong algebraic skills and understanding of proof, as well as building upon prior knowledge on ratio to work with line segments.
prior: Plot coordinates in all four quadrants
Understand gradient and y-intercept in y = mx + c
Interpret real-life contexts with linear graphs

1993.name: Non-linear graphs
1993.description: In this unit graphical representations of non-linear graphs are introduced and explored, and their key features identified.
1993.why: This unit builds upon the preceding unit to incorporate non-linear graphs as well.
prior: Plot and interpret coordinates from equations
Recognise linear and basic quadratic forms
Understand symmetry and turning points

1995.name: 2D and 3D shape: compound shapes
1995.description: In this unit, knowledge of circles and polygons is drawn upon to find the arc length and area of a circle sector and areas of complex compound shapes.
1995.why: This unit is a summation of KS3 work on shape, but extends into parts of a circle and more complicated compound shapes.
prior: Identify and name standard 2D and 3D shapes
Calculate area, perimeter, and volume of standard shapes
Break down complex shapes into known components

1834.name: Angles
1834.description: In this unit pupils use their knowledge of corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles to reason through and solve more complicated problems.
1834.why: This unit builds upon the preceding unit on shape and develops fluency of understanding of angles.
prior: Identify types of angles (acute, obtuse, right, reflex)
Understand angle facts (e.g. angles on a line, around a point)
Use a protractor to measure and draw angles

1997.name: Further transformations
1997.description: In this unit pupils apply their knowledge of transformations to explore negative enlargement factors and the application of multiple transformations.
1997.why: This unit extends knowledge of transformations with combinations of transformations. It purposefully follows extended work on ratios as this is a key skill in this unit.
prior: Identify translations, reflections and rotations
Use vector notation for translations
Describe transformations using appropriate language and coordinates

2001.name: Similarity
2001.description: In this unit, pupils investigate the effect of an enlargement on the perimeter and area of a 2-D shape and the volume of a 3-D shape.
2001.why: This unit builds upon work completed on shape, ratio and transformations.
prior: Recognise congruent shapes
Understand scale factors and enlargement
Use ratio to compare lengths, areas or volumes

1862.name: Plans and elevations
1862.description: In this unit, pupils will be considering a 3-D shape from different viewpoints in order to draw the side and front elevations as well as the plan view.
1862.why: This unit follows on from transformations and further develops spatial awareness.
prior: Identify 2D shapes and 3D solids
Visualise 3D objects from 2D views
Draw front, side, and top elevations

2005.name: Right-angled trigonometry
2005.description: In this unit, pupils are introduced to a variety of situations where trigonometric ratios are required, such as 3-D problems and problems of elevation or depression.
2005.why: This unit requires good understanding of ratios, trigonometric ratios and manipulation of formulae, as such it is positoned after several units revisiting and building upon these key skills.
prior: Identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
Use Pythagoras' Theorem
Understand ratios in similar triangles

1873.name: Bearings
1873.description: In this unit, pupils apply their knowledge of angles in order to calculate bearings and solve angle problems within the context of bearings.
1873.why: This unit requires trigonometry, spatial awareness and angle facts to be able to calculate bearings and reverse bearings. As such it is positioned after those units of work.
prior: Measure angles accurately using a protractor
Use a compass and draw angles from North
Apply knowledge of angles on a straight line and at a point

1977.description: In algebraic manipulation, pupils use apply knowledge of the distributive law to find the product of two binomaials in order to factorise quadratics.

Substitute values into algebraic formulas

Understand scale factors and enlargement

2003.name: Circle theorems
2003.description: In this unit, pupils will use their developed mathematical reasoning skills to derive and use various circle theorems.
2003.why: This is an advanced unit investigating more complex properties of circles, and as such requires in depth knowledge and understanding of shapes, shape properties, proof, angles and ratios.
prior: Identify parts of a circle (radius, diameter, chord, tangent)
Recognise angle facts in triangles and quadrilaterals
Apply geometric reasoning and proof techniques

2010.name: Algebraic fractions
2010.description: In this unit, pupils apply skills in manupulating and solving various equations and formulae to algebraic fractions in order to change the subject and manipulate them.
2010.why: In this unit we are building on a solid foundation of number and algebra skills to extend into algebraic fractions which require strong skills in algebraic manipulation.
prior: Simplify algebraic expressions
Apply fraction rules to algebraic terms
Factor and cancel common algebraic factors

2020.name: 2D and 3D shape: surface area and volume (pyramids, spheres and cones)
2020.description: In this unit, pupils will further develop their understanding of shapes by considering the surface area and volume of pyramids, spheres and cones.
2020.why: This unit continues work on area and volume from the Year 10, introducing more complicated shapes including pyramids, spheres and cones.
prior: Identify and name 2D and 3D shapes
Recall and use area and volume formulas for simple solids

27.belief: 2y and 3y are not like terms because they have different coefficients.

29.correction: 3 lots of 12 isn't 3x10+2 so 3 lots of (y+2) isn't 3y+2. Get students to draw this out. To visualise it.

7589.correction: Correct use of the distributive law with either algebra tiles or an area model will demonstrate why this is wrong.

7738.correction: In order for coordinates to follow a rule written as an equation, there needs to be a relationship between the values within a coordinate.

6838.statement: Pupils may join up their coordinates but not extend their line.
6838.correction: Lines are used to represent all coordinates that follow a rule. Unless given restrictions, lines should be infinitely long.

116.belief: Adding the length of the side onto the wrong value within a coordinate.
116.statement: Adding the length of the side onto the wrong value within a coordinate.
116.correction: Use sketches/ erasable axis/ Desmos to plot points and see if they are reasonable. Encourage writing/drawing on diagrams as working out.

7764.belief: A diamond is an example of a quadrilateral.
7764.statement: Pupils may think a diamond is an example of a quadrilateral.
7764.correction: Rhombus is the correct mathematical name for the shape that pupils may refer to as a diamond.

6254.statement: Pupils may confuse perimeter and area.
6254.correction: Perimeter is the distance around a 2D shape. Area is the size of the surface.

6339.statement: Pupils may not count all sides when calculating the perimeter due to the complexity of the shape.
6339.correction: Encourage pupils to mark the sides as they record the measurement to ensure they count every side length.

7506.statement: Pupils may struggle to think of a different context to apply to finding the perimeter.
7506.correction: An alternative context could be: putting a ribbon around a cake and leaving space for decoration.

7777.belief: They can always double the length and width to calculate the perimeter.
7777.statement: Pupils may think they can always double the length and width to calculate the perimeter.
7777.correction: This only works for composite rectilinear shapes if the lengths do not overlap.

6697.statement: Pupils may forget to halve after multiplying the base and the perpendicular height.
6697.correction: The area of a triangle is equal to half the area of the parallelogram formed by two of those triangles.

7891.belief: The height of the triangle is the slanted height rather than perpendicular.
7891.statement: Pupils may think the height of the triangle is the slanted height rather than perpendicular.
7891.correction: The base and height to be used must be perpendicular (at a right angle) to each other.

728.belief: Breaking the shape into rectangles is always the best approach.
728.statement: Breaking the shape into rectangles is always the best approach.
728.correction: There is not always enough information to use that method so flexible thinking is required.

8428.statement: Pupils may try to combine lengths that are not parallel to a known side length.
8428.correction: For two sets of side lengths to be equal, one set must be parallel to the other and none of the lengths can overlap.

6811.statement: Pupils may incorrectly identify the base of the triangle in the trapezium.
6811.correction: Drawing a trapezium on paper, colouring the sides and cutting it will help them see where the base of the triangle comes from.

6690.statement: Pupils may forget to divide by 2 when calculating the area of a trapezium.
6690.correction: The area of a trapezium is half of the area of the parallelogram formed from two identical trapeziums.

7348.statement: Pupils may struggle to determine whether a question is asking about the perimeter or the area.
7348.correction: Encourage pupils to draw a diagram to represent the situation as this can make it clearer as to whether perimeter or area is required.

2430.belief: When dividing a number line, there is confusion between the intervals and lines.
2430.statement: When dividing a number line, there is confusion between the intervals and lines.
2430.correction: Pupils can write the number on each mark on the number line to ensure equal intervals.

2244.belief: As the denominator is larger the value of the fraction is larger.
2244.statement: As the denominator is larger the value of the fraction is larger.
2244.correction: An analogy of sharing pizza helps students understand. Would pupils get a bigger slice of pizza if it was shared between more people?

4671.belief: A mixed number can be confused with an integer multiplying by the proper fraction.
4671.statement: A mixed number can be confused with an integer multiplying by the proper fraction.
4671.correction: Emphasise the language eg. 3 and a 1/2 means 3 + 1/2.

6943.statement: Some pupils can miscalculate the mixed number to an improper fraction.
6943.correction: For smaller numbers, encourage pupils to draw bar models or diagrams to show the relationship between the whole and the improper fraction.

2245.belief: Denominators that are multiples of 10 will give a terminating decimal.
2245.statement: Denominators that are multiples of 10 will give a terminating decimal.
2245.correction: Investigate the difference between powers of 10 and multiples of 10. e.g 7/30 and 7/100

2036.belief: Converting a fraction to a recurring decimal and then rounding the decimal, gives an accurate answer.
2036.statement: Converting a fraction to a recurring decimal and then rounding the decimal, gives an accurate answer
2036.correction: The use of fractions is more preferred for accuracy than decimals. e.g 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 is not 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.3

2202.belief: The more decimal places there are, the greater the number.
2202.statement: The more decimal places there are, the greater the number.
2202.correction: Pupils can investigate this by looking at the numbers 0.23 and 0.1237 and using a common denominator or 10000.

7869.belief: They just 'get rid' of integers which appear in both numerator and denominator.
7869.statement: Pupils may think they just 'get rid' of integers which appear in both numerator and denominator.
7869.correction: Reinforce that you are multiplying by 1, which doesn't change the value and therefore can be omitted from further calculations.

806.belief: The calculator rounds recurring/non-terminating decimals to 10 d.p. and it is not terminating.
806.statement: The calculator rounds recurring/non-terminating decimals to 10 d.p. and it is not terminating.
806.correction: The fractional form will give a clearer idea if the decimal equivalent is terminating or not.

3703.belief: Incorrect inputting of negative numbers and/or exponents.
3703.statement: Incorrect inputting of negative numbers and/or exponents.
3703.correction: Encourage the use of brackets when using exponents.

53.belief: Just the absolute value is considered and not the integer in its entirety.
53.statement: That just the absolute value is considered and not the integer in its entirety.
53.correction: Encourage pupils to consider the integers as temperatures even if there are no temperature units.

1989.belief: Considering the decimal part of a number to be an integer.
1989.statement: Considering the decimal part of a number to be an integer.
1989.correction: Reinforce the use of a place value table and working from left to right when comparing decimals. It can be useful to use money here.

3145.belief: Fractions with denominators that are not a factors of 10^n cannot be converted into a decimal.
3145.statement: Fractions with denominators that are not a factors of 10^n cannot be converted into a decimal.
3145.correction: This is a good opportunity to reiterate that fractions are an alternative way of writing a division.

1643.belief: Choosing to the find the product of the denominators in order to compare fractions.
1643.statement: Choosing to the find the product of the denominators in order to compare fractions.
1643.correction: Although this is not wrong it can be inefficient. This can be illustrated using large denominators which have a much lower HCF.

3143.belief: Fractions can only be compared using a common denominator.
3143.statement: That fractions can only be compared using a common denominator.
3143.correction: Lots of visual representations are useful here looking at what happens to the size of the 'parts' as the denominator increases.

934.belief: Changing all fractions and decimals to a common format without considering obvious comparisons.
934.statement: Changing all fractions and decimals to a common format without considering obvious comparisons.
934.correction: This could be an opportunity to talk about familiar conversions including halves, quarters and fifths.

2203.belief: When decimals go beyond thousandths you cannot find a number between 2 numbers.
2203.statement: When decimals go beyond thousandths you cannot find a number between 2 numbers.
2203.correction: Use a 'zoomable' number line to show what happens as we zoom in.

463.belief: Assuming that there are 100 minutes in an hour and converting 3.25 hours to 3 hours 25 minutes.
463.statement: Assuming that there are 100 minutes in an hour and converting 3.25 hours to 3 hours 25 minutes.
463.correction: Start with half an hour, pupils should be happy that half an hour is 30 mins, show it written as a decimal to highlight it's not 3.3 hours

9300.belief: Simply adding or subtracting the numerators and denominators.
9300.statement: Simply adding or subtracting the numerators and denominators.
9300.correction: Emphasise that the denominator tells us the name of the unit. In order to add or subtract things they must have a common name.

5339.belief: When partitioning mixed numbers and subtracting incorrectly subtracting the fractional part.
5339.statement: When partitioning mixed numbers and subtracting incorrectly subtracting the fractional part.
5339.correction: Use an integer example to show the structure of partitioning. E.g. 28 - 15 = (20 + 8) - (10 + 5) = (20 - 10) + (8 - 5) not (20 - 10)-(8 - 5)

10607.belief: Use of inefficient methods to multiply fractions, i.e. not considering common factors.
10607.statement: Use of inefficient methods to multiply fractions, i.e. not considering common factors.
10607.correction: The use of fractions with large numerators and denominators can be used to highlight when this is a useful method.

4756.belief: When multiplying a fraction by an integer multiplying the numerator and denominator by the integer.
4756.statement: When multiplying a fraction by an integer multiplying the numerator and denominator by the integer.
4756.correction: If they do this they will have effectively multiplied by 1. Use an example to show you end up with the same fraction that you started with.

3013.belief: Only finding the product of the integers and fractional parts when multiplying mixed numbers.
3013.statement: Only finding the product of the integers and fractional parts when multiplying mixed numbers.
3013.correction: Link back to the area model, there will be 2 parts which they have not found the area of.

2428.belief: When dividing a fraction by an integer, some divide the numerator and denominator by the integer.
2428.statement: When dividing a fraction by an integer, some divide the numerator and denominator by the integer.
2428.correction: Embed the understanding that when dividing by an integer, only the numerator is divided as the number of equal parts remains the same.

10752.belief: Using the unitising method with a remainder, the remainder is not written as a fraction of the unit.
10752.statement: Using the unitising method with a remainder, the remainder is not written as a fraction of the unit.
10752.correction: Drawing bar models, ensure that the unit is subdivided so the remainder can be seen as a fraction of the unit.

5029.belief: Numerators are divided and denominators are divided.
5029.statement: Numerators are divided and denominators are divided.
5029.correction: Emphasize the definition of division. "How many times does.... fit into it?"

5820.belief: Priority of operations does not apply to fractions.
5820.statement: Priority of operations does not apply to fractions
5820.correction: Priority of operations applies to all numbers. They can check with a scientific calculator as the priority of operations is programmed in.

3713.belief: Incorrectly inputting a mixed number into the scientific calculator.
3713.statement: Incorrectly inputting a mixed number into the scientific calculator.
3713.correction: A mixed number has it's own separate button. Incorrectly inputting in the mixed number will return brackets on the calculator screen.

7217.statement: Pupils only see the amount, not proportion. e.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
7217.correction: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.

10713.belief: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
10713.statement: Using multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies of ratios.
10713.correction: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratio tables can help see this more easily.

9172.belief: Only seeing multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies for ratios.
9172.statement: Only seeing multiplication as repeated addition leads to incorrect additive strategies for ratios.
9172.correction: Focus on the multiplicative relationships between parts to whole or whole to parts. Ratios allow the multiplicative relationship to be seen.

7218.statement: Pupils see the bar model and/or fraction as the whole as opposed to the proportion of the whole.
7218.correction: Emphasise equivalent fractions and equivalent bar models which show different parts to whole, but are the same proportion. e.g 3/5 = 60/100

10683.belief: Using additive strategies instead of multiplicative.
10683.statement: Using additive strategies instead of multiplicative.
10683.correction: Emphasise that proportional relationships maintain a constant multiplier so we are looking for a multiplicative relationship.

4215.belief: Both lines of a double number line must start at zero and these zeros must be aligned.
4215.statement: Both lines of a double number line must start at zero and these zeros must be aligned.
4215.correction: When drawing double number lines, ensure to align the zeros and the known equivalents. Showing how a graph is formed from a DNL can help.

2999.belief: To find one part, some students simply divide the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio.
2999.statement: To find one part, some students simply divide the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio.
2999.correction: Strengthen understanding of which amount represents which part of the ratio. Matching problems to bar models helps.

476.belief: An assumption that you cannot find a fraction greater than 1 of an amount.
476.statement: An assumption that you cannot find a fraction greater than 1 of an amount.
476.correction: Recognising that 'of' and multiplication are equivalent should help with this, as pupils are familiar with multiplying fractions.

9170.belief: Only seeing the amount, not proportion. E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
9170.statement: Only seeing the amount, not proportion. E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
9170.correction: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.

9166.belief: Only see the amount, not proportion. E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
9166.statement: Only see the amount, not proportion. E.g £30 from £100 is no different to £30 from £60.
9166.correction: Referring to the whole using bar models or fractions can emphasise the amount with respect to the whole.

2427.belief: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
2427.statement: Always dividing the amount by the sum of the 'parts' of the ratio to get one 'part'.
2427.correction: Offer opportunities to match problems to bar models ensure the same numbers are used to highlight the differences.

9701.belief: Two shapes are congruent based purely on the shape and not the size as well.
9701.statement: Students may believe two shapes are congruent based purely on the shape and not the size as well.
9701.correction: Consider squares - all squares have the same angles and are visually identical but if the lengths are different they're not congruent.

9714.statement: Students may confuse the term transformation for translation.
9714.correction: Translation is one type of transformation.

9723.statement: Students may count between the closest two vertices rather than corresponding points.
9723.correction: Remind frequently that it needs to be between corresponding vertices, labelling may help for this.

9976.statement: Students may translate vertically before horizontally.
9976.correction: Remind the students that the column vectors work in the same way as coordinates.

5043.belief: After an object has been rotated, the orientation stays the same if the image looks the same.
5043.statement: After an object has been rotated, the orientation stays the same if the image looks the same.
5043.correction: This is only true if the object is rotated through 360°. Otherwise, the orientation is different as each vertex is in a different position.

8961.correction: This is only true when referencing the top of the object being rotated. Rotating "left" and "right" is incorrect for all other vertices.

899.belief: The centre of rotation is always in the centre of an object.
899.statement: The centre of rotation is always in the centre of an object.
899.correction: The centre of rotation can be anywhere. If it's outside the shape, imagine it like a pole in the ground, attached to the object by a rope.

2496.belief: After drawing an object on the tracing paper, you take the tracing paper off the table to rotate it.
2496.statement: After drawing an object on the tracing paper, you take the tracing paper off the table to rotate it.
2496.correction: This is especially dangerous if the centre of rotation wasn't drawn on the tracing paper, too. The image will lose its correct location.

591.belief: Just because the sense has changed, it doesn't mean a reflection has occurred.
591.statement: Just because the sense has changed, it doesn't mean a reflection has occurred.
591.correction: If an image has a different sense to its object, there has definitely been a reflection - the line of reflection may be at an obscure angle.

4203.belief: Line segments connecting corresponding points on an image and object can intersect each other.
4203.statement: Line segments connecting corresponding points on an image and object can intersect each other.
4203.correction: Corresponding point line segments after a reflection never intersect. If they do, then corresponding points have not been paired correctly.

2332.belief: Diagonal reflections that incorrectly look like rotations or translations of the object.
2332.statement: Diagonal reflections that incorrectly look like rotations or translations of the object.
2332.correction: False reflections that look like this are due to students not counting diagonals of grid squares, perpendicular to the mirror line.

2696.belief: Enlargement only refers to an increase in size.
2696.statement: Enlargement only refers to an increase in size.
2696.correction: The transformation 'enlargement' refers to a change of size that can be either a stretch or a shrink.

8637.statement: Pupils may want to use division instead of fractional scale factors.
8637.correction: Dividing by 2 gives the same result as multiplying by a half. However, the scale factor is defined as a multiplier, not a divisor.

6828.statement: Pupils may initially be unsure when enlarging shapes on different background in Q2 of Task B.
6828.correction: Stress that they can use the same methods as for square or plain backgrounds (e.g. using a ruler, counting units along gridlines).

9712.statement: Students may confuse reflections and rotations depending on the object.
9712.correction: A reflection is the only transformation that changes the sense of the object, so check that first.

7299.statement: Pupils may struggle with only being able to rotate anticlockwise on Desmos.
7299.correction: Turning clockwise x degrees is equivalent to turning anticlockwise (360 - x) degrees.

5060.belief: There may be occasions when pupils cannot find the tool they are looking for.
5060.statement: There may be occasions when pupils cannot find the tool they are looking for.
5060.correction: Ask them to click 'more' in the toolbar, scroll down and then click 'more' again.

1865.belief: When completing an inverse translation, students may believe they need to flip the vector.
1865.statement: When completing an inverse translation, students may believe they need to flip the vector.
1865.correction: Ask students to say in words how you would return to the starting point, to highlight the direction needed and then link to the vector.

9022.belief: When rounding a number, pupils write the first significant digit(s). e.g 36 789 is 4.
9022.statement: When rounding a number, pupils write the first significant digit(s). e.g 36 789 is 4.
9022.correction: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value.

477.belief: The assumption that if a number ends in 2 zeros it must have been rounded to the nearest hundred.
477.statement: The assumption that if a number ends in 2 zeros it must have been rounded to the nearest hundred.
477.correction: Choose examples that round to the same value when rounded to the nearest ten and hundred in this case. E.g. 398, rounds to 400 to the nearest ten and 400 to the nearest hundred.

2738.belief: Errors when a zero is required when rounding. E.g 5.99 rounds to 6 to 1 d.p.
2738.statement: Errors when a zero is required when rounding. E.g 5.99 rounds to 6 to 1 d.p.
2738.correction: Embedding that 6 and 6.0 may be written like that to convey the accuracy they've been rounded to. To show that 5.99 has been rounded to 1 d.p. we write it as 6.0 not 6.

8207.belief: Repeated rounding gives the correct answer.
8207.statement: Pupils think that repeated rounding gives the correct answer.
8207.correction: Use a number line to support pupils’ understanding. Locate the number to be rounded on the line and identify the critical values.

474.belief: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
474.statement: Assuming all zero digits are not significant.
474.correction: Within the lesson there are many examples where some zeros are significant. Relate significance back to the communication of accuracy and that some digits are significant as they preserve the place value of other digits.

9023.correction: Encourage to use of fractions (where possible) or the use of the ANS button.

2433.belief: Division by 0.5 is the same as doubling.
2433.statement: Division by 0.5 is the same as doubling.
2433.correction: Reiterate the division of a number is the same as the multiplication of the reciprocal e.g The division of 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2. e.g The division of 0.1 is the same as multiplying by 10.

10448.belief: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
10448.statement: When truncating, pupils are tempted to round. Also, when truncating, they cut off the number without thinking about the magnitude.
10448.correction: The use of the place value table shows the magnitude of the number, thus preserving their place value when truncating.

10026.belief: When subtracting or dividing, the largest value is found by subtracting or dividing the upper limit of a number by the upper limit of the divisor or additive inverse.
10026.statement: When subtracting or dividing, the largest value is found by subtracting or dividing the upper limit of a number by the upper limit of the divisor or additive inverse.
10026.correction: Drawing a number line to show with subtraction will help students see how to achieve an upper or lower limits of an error interval calculation. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

3706.belief: Incorrect use of the error interval i.e $$a ≤ x ≤ b$$ or writing the error interval as $$a ≤ x > b$$.
3706.statement: Incorrect use of the error interval i.e $$a ≤ x ≤ b$$ or writing the error interval as $$a ≤ x > b$$
3706.correction: As a check, encourage students to round the upper limit interval by the degree of accuracy to see if it evaluates to the rounded number. Also, draw a number line to show the meaning of $$a ≤ x > b$$ and allow students to see the error.

10759.belief: Using the wrong limits when dividing or subtracting in order to find the upper limit of a calculation or lower limit of a calculation.
10759.statement: Using the wrong limits when dividing or subtracting in order to find the upper limit of a calculation or lower limit of a calculation.
10759.correction: Drawing a number line to show with subtraction will help students see how to achieve an upper or lower limits of an error interval calculation. When using division, reiterating the division of number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

7355.statement: Pupils may struggle to divide values correctly to find a multiplier, especially when fractional.
7355.correction: Pupils should write their sequence out with arrows to show which direction their multiplier is operating.

9213.belief: Sequences can only have constant additive or multiplicative patterns.
9213.statement: That sequences can only have constant additive or multiplicative patterns.
9213.correction: Give students two numbers and get them to carry the sequence on in different ways. Anything they come up with can be a sequence.

6983.statement: Pupils can mix up describing how patterns grow or the relationships between objects in the pattern.
6983.correction: Pupils should verbalise their description, using the keyword 'term', making it clear which way they are describing their pattern.

2346.belief: The difference in the given terms divided by the number of missing terms gives the common difference.
2346.statement: The difference in the given terms divided by the number of missing terms gives the common difference
2346.correction: Write the sequence out with gaps for the missing terms. Model how many additions (jumps) to get from one known term to the next.

5720.belief: The position-to-term rule is the initial term add the common difference.
5720.statement: The position-to-term rule is the initial term add the common difference.
5720.correction: Once pupils have found the additive pattern get them to write each term as a value add the difference.

9216.belief: Sequences such as triangular numbers which have a linear sequence in their differences are linear.
9216.statement: Sequences such as triangular numbers which have a linear sequence in their differences are linear.
9216.correction: Terms in an arithmetic sequence have to have a common first difference.

4804.belief: $$n$$ is a term in the sequence. That $$n=10$$ means 10 is in the sequence.
4804.statement: That $$n$$ is a term in the sequence. That $$n=10$$ means 10 is in the sequence.
4804.correction: Reiterate that $$n$$ is the term number. "$$n=10$$ means the 10th term. What is the 10th term number?"

9208.belief: The sequence $$3n+2$$ starts with 3 and adds 2, or starts with 2 and adds 3.
9208.statement: That the sequence $$3n+2$$ starts with 3 and adds 2, or starts with 2 and adds 3.
9208.correction: Calculate the first few terms. Ask, "When $$n = 1$$ what is the term value?" This is the first value for our sequence.

9209.belief: The sequence 6,11,16,21,... is 5n+6 because it goes up by 5 and starts at 6.
9209.statement: That the sequence 6,11,16,21,... is 5n+6 because it goes up by 5 and starts at 6.
9209.correction: Compare 6,11,16,21,... to 5,10,15,20,... "What is the shift? The translation? If that is 5n then this is 5n with how much more?"

5609.belief: When plotting sequences, a line must be drawn through the points.
5609.statement: When plotting sequences, a line must be drawn through the points.
5609.correction: Plot (1,5), (2,10), (3,15), draw a line and find other coordinates. When n = 1.5 the term value is 7.5. Is 7.5 in the sequence 5n??

3665.belief: It is impossible to tell if 174 368 is in the sequence -8,-3,2,7,...
3665.statement: It is impossible to tell if 174 368 is in the sequence -8,-3,2,7,...
3665.correction: Generalising the rule for forming a given sequence can help us see if a value is in the sequence.

319.belief: The answer to the 'handshake' problem is 15, or 15x15.
319.statement: The answer to the 'handshake' problem is 15, or 15x15
319.correction: Group pupils into 3s and ask them to record how many handshakes are made. Then group as 4s and repeat. What do they notice?

2042.belief: Where is coordinate (−2,5)? 2 down, 5 right from the origin? 5 right, 2 down from the origin?
2042.statement: Where is coordinate (−2,5)? 2 down, 5 right from the origin? 5 right, 2 down from the origin?
2042.correction: Coordinates in (x,y) form. −2 is x-instruction. From (0,0) will we travel in a positive or negative x-direction?

5604.belief: The plotted points of an arithmetic sequence form a line so we draw a line connecting them.
5604.statement: The plotted points of an arithmetic sequence form a line so we draw a line connecting them.
5604.correction: Sequences are an ordered list and do not always need to follow a rule, so we often only find and use the positive integer term numbers.

5607.belief: When plotting the sequence $$3n-1$$ using technology you need to type each coordinate individually.
5607.statement: When plotting the sequence $$3n-1$$ using technology you need to type each coordinate individually.
5607.correction: "We use technology to make things easier. There must be a quicker way!" Look for the 'table' function.

3382.belief: All graphs are linear and if graphs are not linear you join points with straight line segments.
3382.statement: All graphs are linear and if graphs are not linear you join points with straight line segments.
3382.correction: Explore $$n+2, 2n$$ and $$x^2$$. "I see $$n$$ and 2; they must be similar" pupils think. Get them to compare numerically, then graphically.

2718.belief: Only equations in the form $$y=mx+c$$ are linear. All equations are linear.
2718.statement: Only equations in the form $$y=mx+c$$ are linear. All equations are linear.
2718.correction: There are many forms that linear equations can take, however they always share a common feature. The variables have exponents of $$1$$.

378.belief: The arithmetic sequence 5n+2 starts at 7 so the linear equation y=5x+2 'starts' somewhere.
378.statement: The arithmetic sequence 5n+2 starts at 7 so the linear equation y=5x+2 'starts' somewhere.
378.correction: y=5x+2 has no start and no end; it goes on infinitely. However, all linear equations have a y-intercept and this helps define them.

6340.statement: Pupils count squares to calculate gradient instead of looking at scales.
6340.correction: Encourage pupils to pick points on the graph to use to find the gradient and write down the coordinates rather than count squares.

7977.belief: Lines with gradients 2 and -2 are parallel.
7977.statement: Pupils may think lines with gradients 2 and -2 are parallel.
7977.correction: Lines have to have the exact same gradient to be parallel. A line with a negative gradient will intersect a line with a positive gradient.

802.belief: When calculating gradient from coordinates, pupils get positive and negative gradients mixed up.
802.statement: When calculating gradient from coordinates, pupils get positive and negative gradients mixed up.
802.correction: Encourage pupils to sketch the coordinates first and then always look at a positive increase in x.

11167.belief: Writing the y intercept as a single value or getting the x and y coordinates the wrong way around.
11167.statement: Writing the y intercept as a single value or getting the x and y coordinates the wrong way around.
11167.correction: Encourage writing the y intercept as a coordinate. Stating 'lines cross the y axis when x=0' can help pupils write the coordinate correctly.

7879.belief: Graphs are only linear if written in the form y=mx+c.
7879.statement: Pupils may think graphs are only linear if written in the form y=mx+c
7879.correction: Use the first learning cycle as an opportunity to show graphs in many formats. y=mx+c makes the gradient and y intercept clear.

11153.belief: Writing the gradient as the constant and the y intercept as the coefficient of x.
11153.statement: Writing the gradient as the constant and the y intercept as the coefficient of x.
11153.correction: Link to linear sequences where the coefficient of n is the common difference in the sequence to help pupils see why (m) is the gradient.

2489.belief: To draw the graph using the gradient and intercept you can just count the squares.
2489.statement: To draw the graph using the gradient and intercept you can just count the squares.
2489.correction: Encourage pupils to look at the scales on the axes carefully when drawing a line given the gradient and y-intercept.

4205.belief: From the line $$y=x$$ to $$y=x+1$$ to $$y=x-1$$ the lines are moving left/right rather than up/down.
4205.statement: From the line $$y=x$$ to $$y=x+1$$ to $$y=x-1$$ the lines are moving left/right rather than up/down.
4205.correction: It can be shown by using a $$(x,c)$$ coordinate in desmos. That coordinate moves up and down with the change in '$$c$$'.

5116.belief: There is one answer to everything in maths.
5116.statement: There is one answer to everything in maths.
5116.correction: We often see arithmetic and equations with one answer but, maths can be used to compare and justify multiple answers to a single problem.

2035.belief: When converting English to algebra, pupils can mix up 4x + 2 and 4(x + 2).
2035.statement: When converting English to algebra, pupils can mix up 4x + 2 and 4(x + 2)
2035.correction: Reviewing priority of operations and expanding brackets may be helpful. The multiplier operates on all terms in the bracket.

10452.belief: Trying to double an expression and only doubling one term.
10452.statement: Trying to double an expression and only doubling one term.
10452.correction: Use the numerical examples to show why this does not work. Use of brackets in working out is also helpful.

7813.belief: All equations are for straight lines so can be plotted from 2 points.
7813.statement: Pupils may think all equations are for straight lines so can be plotted from 2 points.
7813.correction: Explore different relationships, most relationships are not linear but we focus a lot on linear relationships and their unique structure.

10.correction: Using bar models can help pupils understand rearranging additive relationships at an early stage.

8777.belief: When reading solutions from a graph pupils may read the solution as the y-coordinate.
8777.statement: When reading solutions from a graph pupils may read the solution as the y-coordinate.
8777.correction: The solution to the equation is the value of the variable that makes both sides balance.

8351.belief: A value has to be added to each term in an expression.
8351.statement: Pupils may think a value has to be added to each term in an expression.
8351.correction: When adding a term to an expression we can write it as a single addition and then collect like terms if necessary. Show with numbers first

9423.belief: When solving x - 5 = 10 pupils may see the -5 and calculate 10 - 5 = 5.
9423.statement: When solving x - 5 = 10 pupils may see the -5 and calculate 10 - 5 = 5
9423.correction: Focus on understanding zero pairs and why adding the additive inverse gives the solution. Bar models are a helpful representation here.

9420.belief: When solving equations pupils may not use the inverse operation.
9420.statement: When solving equations pupils may not use the inverse operation.
9420.correction: Working out should include each step then pupils can check each step using substitution.

8539.statement: Pupils can be unsure which values to add and which to subtract when collecting like terms.
8539.correction: Rewrite the equation with like terms grouped together before combining like terms.

5195.belief: There is only one way to solve any given equation.
5195.statement: That there is only one way to solve any given equation.
5195.correction: In maths we will often see multiple ways to solve the same one problem. To be able to use multiple methods is a demonstration of fluency.

10022.belief: To subtract from both the variable and numerical terms when subtracting from both sides.
10022.statement: To subtract from both the variable and numerical terms when subtracting from both sides.
10022.correction: To subtract $$2$$ from $$5x+3$$ leaves $$5x+1$$, not $$3x+1$$. Use visual representations like balance scales and bar models to show this.

7008.statement: Pupils often "multiply through by $$5$$" and turn $${{2x+1}\over5}={10}$$ into $${{10x+5}}={50}$$
7008.correction: Use equivalent fractions as opposed to multiplying through. In one simple step $${{2x+1}\over5}={10}$$ becomes $${{2x+1}\over5}={50\over5}$$

11174.belief: "$$x$$ times five, plus three" is the same as "$$x$$ plus three, times five".
11174.statement: That "$$x$$ times five, plus three" is the same as "$$x$$ plus three, times five".
11174.correction: Use visual representations to demonstrate why and how they are different. Use algebra tiles if you have them, or get pupils to draw them.

719.belief: All brackets have to be expanded before we solve an equation with brackets it in.
719.statement: That all brackets have to be expanded before we solve an equation with brackets it in.
719.correction: How would you solve $$2y=50$$? You would divide both sides by $$2$$. So why not start with 'divide $$2$$' when solving $$2(y-7)=50$$?

10670.belief: We always have to use written methods to solve equations.
10670.statement: That we always have to use written methods to solve equations.
10670.correction: Use Desmos to show that equations like $$3x-1=17$$ and $$3x-1=x+9$$ can be solved by drawing both lines and finding the intersection.

215.belief: Algebra, in particular solving equations, is abstract and not related to the world around us.
215.statement: That algebra, in particular solving equations, is abstract and not related to the world around us.
215.correction: Ask pupils to solve $$4(x+3)=20$$. Then show a square with length $$x+3$$, tell them the perimeter is $$20$$ and ask them to find $$x$$.

3003.belief: When finding 10% we divide by 10, so when finding 5% we divide by 5.
3003.statement: When finding 10% we divide by 10, so when finding 5% we divide by 5.
3003.correction: Use a bar model to show the division of 10 means one tenth of the amount. When dividing by 5 it means one fifth has been found.

3710.belief: Incorrectly drawing a scaled axis is common.
3710.statement: Incorrectly drawing a scaled axis is common.
3710.correction: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference bewteen the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2.

9337.belief: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3.
9337.statement: A single digit percentage is incorrectly worked out by dividing by 10 and not 100 e.g 3% = 0.3
9337.correction: Two responses can be used to remind students that to covert a percentage into a decimal; we divide by 100; using 3%, ask what 30% is as a decimal and 3% as a decimal. Pupils realise they cannot be the same. A place value chart also helps.

5926.belief: Pupil can often get confused with increasing and decreasing an amount e.g Increase 45 by 23% and decreasing 45 by 23% have the same multiplier.
5926.statement: Pupil can often get confused with increasing and decreasing an amount e.g Increase 45 by 23% and decreasing 45 by 23% have the same multiplier.
5926.correction: Encourage students to draw double number lines or ratio tables so they can see the increase and multiplier or decrease and multiplier.

3097.belief: Forgetting to find the percentage change.
3097.statement: Forgetting to find the percentage change.
3097.correction: Emphasise the word change. Encourage pupils to write down the 2 percentages with their relevant values. Go back to the question and calculate the actual change they should notice that this is neither of the 2 values but the difference between them.

3709.belief: Incorrectly drawing or interpreting the scales on axes.
3709.statement: Incorrectly drawing or interpreting the scales on axes.
3709.correction: Use the approach where pupils count the number of intervals of the scale and divide the difference between the intervals. For example, if there are 5 intervals and the difference is between 20 and 30, they divide 10 by 2, so each interval is 2

468.belief: Assuming that any graph with a constant positive gradient represents variables that are in direct proportion.
468.statement: Assuming that any graph with a constant positive gradient represents variables that are in direct proportion.
468.correction: Encourage the useful check of reading a pairs of values from the graph, doubling one of them and checking the graph to see if the other variable has doubled. If it has it shows a directly proportional relationship if not it doesn't.

464.belief: Assuming that to convert 1 metre squared to cm squared you multiply by 100 and not 10 000.
464.statement: Assuming that to convert 1 metre squared to cm squared you multiply by 100 and not 10 000
464.correction: Encourage any pupil who initially finds this challenging to ensure that the values are in the required unit for the answer before doing the calculation.

3373.belief: The graph representing a inversely proportional relationship is of the form x + y = a and will eventually meet the axes.
3373.statement: The graph representing a inversely proportional relationship is of the form x + y = a and will eventually meet the axes.
3373.correction: The dimensions of the rectangle are ideal for highlighting this, particularly the latter part as a you cannot have a rectangle with a length of 0 cm.

6702.statement: Pupils may forget the key with a pictogram or mislabel the vertical scale for bar charts.
6702.correction: By asking the pupils how they know there are 'x things', to highlight the need for the key.

3575.belief: The icon that the pupils choose is too complicated to duplicate and cannot be divided well.
3575.statement: The icon that the pupils choose is too complicated to duplicate and cannot be divided well.
3575.correction: Have the pupils try and find an icon with reflective symmetry and simple shapes.

6873.statement: Pupils may label the vertical axis with the frequency values rather than a scale.
6873.correction: Remind the pupils that the scale should go up in the same jumps. i.e. 0, 5, 10, 15 etc and have them check theirs.

7243.statement: Pupils may select additional cells which will cause their chart to look strange.
7243.correction: They can edit the data selected or delete the chart and start again.

3173.belief: The frequencies on the frequency table are the angles you plot onto the pie chart.
3173.statement: The frequencies on the frequency table are the angles you plot onto the pie chart.
3173.correction: Challenge the misconception by using an example with frequencies that clearly add to more or less than 360 e.g. {90, 90, 180, 90, 60)

4.belief: 1) = not necessary to put into function, 2) students type in number to calculate, not click the cell.
4.statement: 1) = not necessary to put into function, 2) students type in number to calculate, not click the cell
4.correction: 1) the = at the start tells the spreadsheet to start a calculation, 2) clicking the cell means if input data chances, outputs auto-update

10478.belief: Two sectors on two different pie charts that have the same angle represent the same frequency.
10478.statement: Two sectors on two different pie charts that have the same angle represent the same frequency.
10478.correction: 90° of a pie chart of 4 data points represents less frequency (frequency of 1) than 90° of a pie chart of 200 data points (frequency of 50).

10143.belief: Task B Q2 - Pupils may choose to go up in 100s on the vertical axis.
10143.statement: Task B Q2 - Pupils may choose to go up in 100s on the vertical axis.
10143.correction: Highlight that all of their data points will be in the bottom half of the graph and suggest going up in 50s.

7311.statement: Pupils may struggle to assign the correct variable to the y-axis when graphing on a spreadsheet.
7311.correction: Explain that the word "series" is used to mean the y-axis in this software.

5976.belief: All there is always a connection between variables in scatter graphs.
5976.statement: Pupils may assume that all there is always a connection between variables in scatter graphs.
5976.correction: Emphasise examples showing no/weak connections, but explain that the tasks use data containing stronger connections for purpose of practice.

7752.belief: Data is only presented using the types of graphs that they learn in school.
7752.statement: Pupils may think that data is only presented using the types of graphs that they learn in school.
7752.correction: Data can presented visually in anyway that helps people to understand it. Explore other types of graphs and infographics used in the media.

6789.statement: Pupils may ignore a data point of zero in their calculation of the mean.
6789.correction: Data points of zero will not add to the total but does impact the number of values, so the mean will be incorrect with its omission.

6371.statement: Pupils may divide by how many groups/bars there are, instead of the total frequency.
6371.correction: By reminding students frequently that averages need to give a 'typical' value of the data set, ask them to sense check their mean value.

6258.statement: Pupils may confuse the position of the median with the median's actual value.
6258.correction: Choose data where the position number would not be a reasonable median value and ensure pupils sense check their answers every time.

6187.statement: Pupils may choose the middle bar on the bar chart or the middle value on the x-axis as their median.
6187.correction: Pull off the data from the bar chart or line graph to show where the median value is.

8498.statement: Pupils may not understand what feature of a data set they're trying to find when identifying a mode
8498.correction: Phrase the question as 'What is the modal colour?' for instance, rather than just 'What is the mode?'

6977.statement: Pupils may mistakenly choose the bars which have the same heights to be the mode.
6977.correction: By reminding the pupils of the definition of the mode and asking the question in the context of the data, this should support students.

8664.statement: Pupils may often write the range as '3 to 10' or '10 - 3' rather than a single value.
8664.correction: Remind pupils that the range is a single value which describes how far apart the extreme values are.

4512.belief: The mean is the most meaningful average.
4512.statement: The mean is the most meaningful average.
4512.correction: Looking at bimodal data, trimodal data or data with extreme outliers. Context may be relevant.

514.belief: Averages (mean, median, mode) will always change if a data point needs to be added, removed, edited.
514.statement: Averages (mean, median, mode) will always change if a data point needs to be added, removed, edited.
514.correction: The mean, median, or mode will remain invariant if a data point is added with the same value as that average.

120.belief: "Adding or removing a data point from a dataset will always change the value of the range".
120.statement: "Adding or removing a data point from a dataset will always change the value of the range"
