120.correction: The range only changes if: the data point added becomes a new max or min value, or the data point removed is the current max or min value.

5515.belief: Pie charts but not bar charts can show what proportion of a dataset a particular subgroup represents.
5515.statement: Pie charts but not bar charts can show what proportion of a dataset a particular subgroup represents
5515.correction: You can figure out proportion from a bar chart by comparing the frequency of one subgroup to the total frequency, by adding heights of bars.

10465.belief: If two datasets have the same mean, then the distribution of data points will look similar.
10465.statement: If two datasets have the same mean, then the distribution of data points will look similar.
10465.correction: Even with the same mean, two datasets could have vastly different ranges. One dataset could be bimodal, whilst the other could be unimodal.

4513.belief: The mean and median will always be close to the most frequent values (or peaks) in a dataset.
4513.statement: The mean and median will always be close to the most frequent values (or peaks) in a dataset.
4513.correction: The mean and median may be at the lower or lowest frequency parts of a distribution. This is especially likely if the data is bimodal.

2054.belief: Correlation always means that one of the variables is affecting the other variable.
2054.statement: Correlation always means that one of the variables is affecting the other variable.
2054.correction: Correlation only suggests variables may be related somehow. Show examples where variables correlate because they both depend on population.

11082.belief: The word 'population' always refers to the entire population of a country or the world.
11082.statement: The word 'population' always refers to the entire population of a country or the world.
11082.correction: The population in a given context is defined by the entire set of people/creatures/items that are being considered.

2609.belief: Either the mean, median or mode could be used as an average in any situation.
2609.statement: Either the mean, median or mode could be used as an average in any situation.
2609.correction: The choice of average can depend on the type of data. For example, in a list of colours, you can find the mode but not the mean.

4892.belief: You always need to start the axis of a scatter graph at (0,0).
4892.statement: You always need to start the axis of a scatter graph at (0,0).
4892.correction: The axis of a scatter graph should use a scale that makes the points as clear to see as possible, without distorting the shape of the data.

3015.belief: The findings for a data investigation using a sample can always be generalised to the population.
3015.statement: The findings for a data investigation using a sample can always be generalised to the population.
3015.correction: The generalisability of results can depend on how representative the sample is of the population which it is being compared to.

8893.belief: Reporting two averages when asked to make two comparisons between sets of data.
8893.statement: Reporting two averages when asked to make two comparisons between sets of data.
8893.correction: Mean, media and mode essentially measure the same thing: central tendency. So use one of the comparisons to comment on the spread of data.

10047.belief: Summing all of the given lengths and only the given lengths to find the perimeter.
10047.statement: Summing all of the given lengths and only the given lengths to find the perimeter.
10047.correction: With each example discuss which lengths are part of the perimeter, which lengths are not and whether any lengths are equal to others.

6467.statement: Pupils may find the area by multiplying lengths which are not perpendicular.
6467.correction: Area is measured in square units. The base and height of a square are perpendicular. We multiply perpendicular lengths to make square units.

8303.belief: The π symbol represents a variable, similar to letters such as r and d.
8303.statement: Pupils may think that the π symbol represents a variable, similar to letters such as r and d.
8303.correction: Reiterate the difference between variables and constants. Explain that while the radius may differ between circles, π is always the same.

11143.belief: When writing answers in terms of π, pupils may think that π is the units.
11143.statement: When writing answers in terms of π, pupils may think that π is the units.
11143.correction: π is a constant and makes up part of the numerical component of the answer. Units (such as square metres) still need to be stated.

6233.statement: Pupils may confuse the formula for area with the 2πr version of the formula for circumference.
6233.correction: Area is a 2-dimensional space so its formula requires the multiplication of two lengths. This happens when we square the radius.

799.belief: When calculating the diameter, pupils may use rounded numbers to perform subsequent calculations.
799.statement: When calculating the diameter, pupils may use rounded numbers to perform subsequent calculations.
799.correction: Repeat one of the demonstrations of finding the diameter but round each decimal as they appear and compare the accuracy of the final answer.

2993.belief: To find the area of a quarter-circle divide the radius by 4 to use as part of the calculation.
2993.statement: To find the area of a quarter-circle divide the radius by 4 to use as part of the calculation.
2993.correction: You must divide the area by 4, not the radius. The radius gets squared when calculating area so the division of r would be applied twice.

9249.belief: Shapes with the same area also have the same perimeter.
9249.statement: Shapes with the same area also have the same perimeter.
9249.correction: Demonstrate that component parts being rearranged has no effect on its area, but may affect its perimeter.

10908.belief: If I want to find the radius of a semicircle from its area, I halve the area first.
10908.statement: If I want to find the radius of a semicircle from its area, I halve the area first.
10908.correction: You must double the area. This calculates the area of a full circle, whose radius can be found by first dividing by π, then square rooting.

385.belief: Any arrangement of 6 square-faces will result in the net of a cube.
385.statement: Any arrangement of 6 square-faces will result in the net of a cube.
385.correction: Some arrangements of 6 squares will result in some of them overlapping when the shape is folded into 3D, resulting in an incomplete cube.

10164.belief: I can tell a 3D shape is a prism because the 2D faces on both ends are congruent.
10164.statement: I can tell a 3D shape is a prism because the 2D faces on both ends are congruent.
10164.correction: The cross-sectional face must be the same throughout, not just at the two ends of the shape. Also, the two end faces must be parallel.

8426.statement: Pupils may try to avoid sketching of nets or faces and in turn miss information.
8426.correction: Reassure pupils that a sketch does not need to be perfect and just needs to convey the key information.

7057.statement: Pupils may overlook whether they have been given the diameter or radius of the circles.
7057.correction: Encourage pupils to always write down the radius before any calculation of the surface area is started.

7014.statement: Pupils may multiply all lengths on the diagram rather than find the area of the cross-section.
7014.correction: Draw the cross-sectional polygon out, find the area and then multiply by the length of the prism.

7013.statement: Pupils may multiply the length and radius before squaring.
7013.correction: Remind students of the order of operations and link to the volume of a prism formula: finding the area of the cross-section first.

7345.statement: Pupils may struggle to decide whether the question is needing length, area or volume.
7345.correction: Support could be given by providing the units for the answer or pupils may be encouraged to think of contexts for each before hand.

5239.belief: In order for two angles to be supplementary, they must both lie about a point on a straight line.
5239.statement: In order for two angles to be supplementary, they must both lie about a point on a straight line.
5239.correction: For two angles to be supplementary, they must sum to 180°. They do not also need to both lie on a straight line.

278.belief: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
278.statement: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°
278.correction: Angles on a straight line only sum to 180° if all of those angles share a common vertex. Show two angles "on a line" at different points.

3529.belief: The horizontal side length of an isosceles triangle is always the base side.
3529.statement: The horizontal side length of an isosceles triangle is always the base side.
3529.correction: The base side of an isosceles triangle can have any orientation. It is important to look at the hash marks, angle markers, or measurements.

2487.belief: I can draw a 7 cm line with my ruler.
2487.statement: I can draw a 7 cm line with my ruler.
2487.correction: A line is a linear path that continues forever in both directions. We can draw line segments with a ruler, which have distinct endpoints.

10415.belief: Transversals must intersect a pair of parallel lines.
10415.statement: Transversals must intersect a pair of parallel lines.
10415.correction: Transversals can intersect any set of lines or line segments, no matter whether any of those lines or line segments are parallel or not.

8821.belief: Referring to alternate angles as 'Z' angles because of the arrangement of the lines.
8821.statement: Referring to alternate angles as 'Z' angles because of the arrangement of the lines.
8821.correction: Modelling the justification correctly through every example and using exterior alternate angles to highlight the limitations of 'Z' angles.

6051.belief: The co-interior angles are equal, like alternate and corresponding angles.
6051.statement: Pupils may believe that the co-interior angles are equal, like alternate and corresponding angles.
6051.correction: Have pupils draw a pair of parallel lines and a transversal line themselves, identify the co-interior angles, are they equal?

7415.statement: Pupils may struggle with the justifications rather than getting to the answer.
7415.correction: Keep asking pupils "why?" and encourage them to ask themselves, whenever they are working out an angle.

7436.statement: Pupils may struggle with mathematical proof, especially using other knowledge within it.
7436.correction: Explain to pupils that there are many different styles of mathematical proof but all are showing that a particular fact holds true for all.

473.belief: Assuming triangles are certain types because of how they look.
473.statement: Assuming triangles are certain types because of how they look.
473.correction: Unless there is notation or it has stated the type of triangle you cannot assume.

9559.belief: When splitting a polygon into triangles, pupils may draw line segments that cross inside the shape.
9559.statement: When splitting a polygon into triangles, pupils may draw line segments that cross inside the shape.
9559.correction: By choosing a single common vertex for all the triangles, the line segments will not cross inside the shape.

3824.belief: Interior angles always sum to 180 times the number of component triangles it is split into.
3824.statement: Interior angles always sum to 180 times the number of component triangles it is split into.
3824.correction: If line segments drawn make new vertices in the polygon, its angles won't contribute to the sum of interior angles in the initial polygon.

2875.belief: The exterior angle is the entire reflex angle that is on the outside of each vertex of a shape.
2875.statement: The exterior angle is the entire reflex angle that is on the outside of each vertex of a shape.
2875.correction: Ask a pupil to stand and walk around the room to trace a shape. The angle that the pupil turns at each vertex is an exterior angle.

7257.statement: Pupils may solve angle problems by using methods which are less efficient than others.
7257.correction: While less efficient methods are fine, encourage pupils to review their work each time they solve a problem to consider alternative methods.

8650.statement: Pupils may work out missing angles without writing out their justifications.
8650.correction: Each time a number which is not on the original diagram is used or found, an explanation should be given for where it has come from.

6867.statement: Pupils might not know how to start an angle problem if they focus too much on the final solution.
6867.correction: You can start an angle problem by working out any angle on the diagram. The more angles you work out, the easier the final solution becomes.

2491.belief: When drawing circles, pupils may find that the start and end of their arcs do not join together.
2491.statement: When drawing circles, pupils may find that the start and end of their arcs do not join together.
2491.correction: This can be caused by the pair of compasses opening or closing mid-drawing. Hold it with one hand and rest the pencil gently on the page.

6546.statement: Pupils may find it difficult to decide where to mark the centre point of each circle during Task A.
6546.correction: Pupils could start the task by drawing a pair of circles and labelling it with the question that presents the matching description.

10150.belief: During tasks, pupils may use a ruler to draw or check whether points are equidistant from a centre.
10150.statement: During tasks, pupils may use a ruler to draw or check whether points are equidistant from a centre.
10150.correction: While the tasks could be completed with a ruler, it may be quicker, easier and more accurate to use a pair of compasses.

6022.statement: Pupils may avoid using the pair of compasses and opt for a ruler instead.
6022.correction: Emphasise the efficiency and accuracy of using compasses instead of a ruler in the construction of their triangles.

7349.statement: Pupils may struggle with a diagonal of a shape being vertical or horizontal.
7349.correction: By reminding pupils of the definition, ask them to check if it fits and the shape could be rotated as well.

10631.belief: I can use a protractor to measure an angle, then half that angle to bisect it.
10631.statement: I can use a protractor to measure an angle, then half that angle to bisect it.
10631.correction: Constructions, such as bisecting an angle, are methods of creating & modifying shapes & angles in ways that don't require measurement tools.

10634.belief: I can use a ruler to measure the midpoint of a line segment, and a protractor to find 90°.
10634.statement: I can use a ruler to measure the midpoint of a line segment, and a protractor to find 90°.
10634.correction: Constructions, such as perpendicular bisectors, are methods of creating & modifying shapes & angles in ways that don't require measurements.

832.belief: You can't accurately draw the perpendicular to a point on a line segment close to its endpoint.
832.statement: You can't accurately draw the perpendicular to a point on a line segment close to its endpoint.
832.correction: The perpendicular to a line segment through any point can be found; some line segments just require extending in length first.

4858.belief: You always need to draw circles that are the same size to construct any polygon.
4858.statement: You always need to draw circles that are the same size to construct any polygon.
4858.correction: Some polygons, such as kites, require you to construct two circles of different size, as long as they still intersect at two points.

5304.belief: When a pair of similar shapes are not in the same orientation, pupils may select an incorrect pair of lengths to calculate the scale factor.
5304.statement: When a pair of similar shapes are not in the same orientation, pupils may select an incorrect pair of lengths to calculate the scale factor.
5304.correction: Encourage pupils to take a systematic approach to locating pairs of corresponding lengths by looking for the longest edge in each shape, then the second longest, third longest, etc.

6562.statement: Pupils may find it difficult to match up corresponding measurements on two congruent shapes when they are in different orientations.
6562.correction: Look lengths which are between any pairs of known angles or look for angles which are between pairs of adjacent known lengths. Also, tracing paper could be used to reflect/rotate/translate one shape onto the other.

7810.belief: They do not have enough information about a shape to determine whether it is congruent to another shape, when in fact they do.
7810.statement: Pupils may think that they do not have enough information about a shape to determine whether it is congruent to another shape, when in fact they do.
7810.correction: Pupils could attempt the draw the shape based on the information that they have. They can then consider whether there are multiple way that the shape can be drawn while still satisfying all the given information.

6990.statement: Pupils may mix up the meanings of congruence and similarity or struggle with the hierarchy of their nested sets (e.g. thinking that all similar shapes are congruent rather than the other way around).
6990.correction: Frequently refer to a Venn diagram showing the set of congruence shapes inside the set of similar shapes when examining pairs of shapes.

9019.belief: When rotating a shape to count its order of rotational symmetry, pupils may count the starting position twice: once at the start and then again at the end of the full turn.
9019.statement: When rotating a shape to count its order of rotational symmetry, pupils may count the starting position twice: once at the start and then again at the end of the full turn.
9019.correction: Encourage pupils to be consistent with when they count the starting position, either always counting it before they begin rotating the shape or always counting it at the end of the full turn.

6132.belief: As the sides fix the angles, that this implies it is true conversely.
6132.statement: Pupils may believe that as the sides fix the angles, that this implies it is true conversely.
6132.correction: Use any regular polygon to highlight that the angles will always be the same, but the edge lengths are not always the same length. Regular polygons are always similar but not necessarily congruent.

6040.belief: The angle doesn't need to be in between the two known sides.
6040.statement: Pupils may believe that the angle doesn't need to be in between the two known sides.
6040.correction: Use the Geogebra files to demonstrate that more than one triangle can be formed at times, and therefore it does not guarantee congruence between two triangles.

7495.statement: Pupils may struggle to spot congruent triangles if they only look for ASA.
7495.correction: Encourage pupils to add any further information to diagrams, like the third angle, before starting to prove congruence.

6907.statement: Pupils may make assumptions about diagrams containing a right angle incorrectly.
6907.correction: Remind pupils, that they cannot assume there is a right angle, just because it may look like the two edges are perpendicular to each other.

8038.belief: They need to know the actual size or length to be able to prove congruence.
8038.statement: Pupils may think they need to know the actual size or length to be able to prove congruence.
8038.correction: Remind pupils that if they can show that the corresponding angles or sides are the same length, then that is all that is needed. For example, if the corresponding edges are both edges of the same regular polygon, then they will be the same.

8682.belief: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
8682.statement: Pythagoras' theorem is just a relationship between the three sides of a right-angled triangle.
8682.correction: Whilst this is true, Pythagoras' theorem can more visually be represented as three squares whose sides are equal in length to the three sides of the triangle. The sum of the areas of the two smaller squares is equal to the area of the larger square.

8683.belief: Pythagorean triples can be a trio of any rational numbers that, when constructed into a triangle, always produces a right-angled triangle.
8683.statement: Pythagorean triples can be a trio of any rational numbers that, when constructed into a triangle, always produces a right-angled triangle.
8683.correction: Pythagorean triples are conventionally a trio of integer side lengths of a right-angled triangle, such as the 3, 4, 5 triangle. Other, similar triangles can be generated from Pythagorean triples, whose side lengths are rational, such as 0.3, 0.4, 0.5

4583.belief: The method for finding the length of a shorter side of a right-angled triangle using Pythagoras' theorem is exactly the same as when finding the hypotenuse.
4583.statement: The method for finding the length of a shorter side of a right-angled triangle using Pythagoras' theorem is exactly the same as when finding the hypotenuse.
4583.correction: Whilst the initial setup of "the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides equals the square of the hypotenuse" will be the same, finding the length of a shorter side will require an extra step of rearranging terms in the equation.

10632.belief: I can only use Pythagoras' theorem to find the length of a side of a right-angled triangle when the right-angle marker is labelled, so I know which side is the hypotenuse.
10632.statement: I can only use Pythagoras' theorem to find the length of a side of a right-angled triangle when the right-angle marker is labelled, so I know which side is the hypotenuse.
10632.correction: The right-angle marker doesn't need to be explicitly labelled in order to be able to identify the right-angle. You can use knowledge of "interior angles in a triangle sum to 180°" to find the right angle, given two other angles.

4863.belief: I need to be given a triangle in order to use Pythagoras' theorem.
4863.statement: I need to be given a triangle in order to use Pythagoras' theorem.
4863.correction: You do not need to be given a triangle. It is an important skill to be able to sketch and label a triangle for yourself from given information, or go straight into an algebraic stage of calculation if aware that lengths given are perpendicular.

8706.belief: Every question that has a right-angled triangle must use Pythagoras' theorem to be solved.
8706.statement: Every question that has a right-angled triangle must use Pythagoras' theorem to be solved.
8706.correction: It is easy to get into a habit of using Pythagoras' theorem when learning the topic, but it is likely you have seen several maths problems in the past with right-angled triangles, which ask to find areas and angles, without using Pythagoras' theorem.

8996.belief: Rolling a 6 on a dice is less likely to happen than rolling other numbers. Or ticket 001 is less likely to be drawn in a raffle than other tickets.
8996.statement: Rolling a 6 on a dice is less likely to happen than rolling other numbers. Or ticket 001 is less likely to be drawn in a raffle than other tickets.
8996.correction: The random nature of picking a raffle or rolling a dice means all outcomes are equally likely as each other.

5282.belief: The outcomes of a trial are always equally likely to occur (e.g. each of the two players in a tennis match are equally likely to win).
5282.statement: The outcomes of a trial are always equally likely to occur (e.g. each of the two players in a tennis match are equally likely to win).
5282.correction: There are factors that may affect how likely one outcome is compared to another (e.g. the skill or experience of one tennis player compared to the other).

2713.belief: 'Equal chance' means the same as 'even chance'.
2713.statement: 'Equal chance' means the same as 'even chance'.
2713.correction: When a trial has more than two possible outcomes which are all equally likely to happen, each outcome has less than an even chance of happening. E.g. each number on a dice has the same likelihood of being rolled, but each is less than an even chance.

9373.belief: A small number of trials in an experiment is enough to provide conclusive findings.
9373.statement: A small number of trials in an experiment is enough to provide conclusive findings.
9373.correction: Even in situations where we know that the different outcomes of a trial are equally likely happen, one outcome may happen more often than the others. E.g. when we flip a coin 10 times, we don't always get the exact same number of heads and tails.

8621.statement: Pupils want to avoid writing lists of outcomes.
8621.correction: Always model and bring explicit attention to a systematic list. The benefits of working systematically is the likelihood of error is reduced.

8652.statement: Pupils may worry about which event/stage of the trial should be the rows and which should be the columns in an outcome table.
8652.correction: Explain that the rows and columns can be transposed. Depending on the context AB and BA may be the same outcome, whereas in other contexts they may be two different outcomes, so a little care is needed in interpretation.

3408.belief: Every group of branches should have the same number of branches.
3408.statement: Every group of branches should have the same number of branches.
3408.correction: In a multi-staged trial, each stage may have a different number of outcomes. The number of branches in each group reflects the number of outcomes of a stage. This means each group of branches can be made from a different number of branches.

6394.statement: Pupils may not draw the rectangle in their Venn diagrams.
6394.correction: Refer back to the rectangle hosting all possible outcomes; the sample space and therefore a vital part of a Venn diagram.

5280.belief: An outcome tree doesn't have a sample space.
5280.statement: An outcome tree doesn't have a sample space.
5280.correction: Each representation of the outcomes of a trial have a sample space as a part of it. For an outcome table, the table itself is the sample space. For an outcome tree, a sample space must always be constructed after drawing the two layers of branches.

5281.belief: An outcome tree can only have a maximum of three layers of branches.
5281.statement: An outcome tree can only have a maximum of three layers of branches.
5281.correction: An outcome tree can have as many layers of branches as needed, depending on the number of stages there are in a trial. For example, if a trial involved flipping 7 coins, then there would be 7 layers of branches! That's too probably too many to draw!

7443.statement: Pupils may struggle with the phrasing and language, when trying to identify the correct regions of the Venn diagram.
7443.correction: Encourage the pupils to describe each region of the Venn diagram, in context where appropriate.

10624.belief: I can use outcome tables to categorise outcomes into as many events as I want.
10624.statement: I can use outcome tables to categorise outcomes into as many events as I want.
10624.correction: Outcome tables are limited to categorising outcomes into only two events. You can use more tables to categorise outcomes into three or more events, but the number of tables you need quickly becomes massive!

5279.belief: Outcome tables and outcome trees only work for outcomes that are all equally likely.
5279.statement: Outcome tables and outcome trees only work for outcomes that are all equally likely.
5279.correction: Outcome tables can be separated into more rows and columns, and outcome trees split into more branches, to show outcomes that are more or less likely than other ones. This does mean these diagrams do get massive very quickly!

6892.statement: Pupils may list the possible outcomes in an unsystematic way, potentially causing them to miss or repeat outcomes.
6892.correction: Demonstrate how our system of counting is a systematic method for listing numbers and compare it to some of the listing strategies used in the lesson.

7974.belief: 'likely' from the scale of likelihoods is only equal to a specific probability (e.g. 75%).
7974.statement: Pupils think that 'likely' from the scale of likelihoods is only equal to a specific probability (e.g. 75%).
7974.correction: All probabilities that are greater than 50% but less than 100% are equivalent to 'likely' on the scale of likelihoods.

6002.belief: Theoretical probabilities can be also found in cases where individual outcomes are not equally likely (e.g. picking a sweet out of a box where the sweets are different shapes).
6002.statement: Pupils may assume that theoretical probabilities can be also found in cases where individual outcomes are not equally likely (e.g. picking a sweet out of a box where the sweets are different shapes).
6002.correction: If the sweets in a box are different shapes then picking a sweet out of the box is not necessarily random. Someone could find their favourite flavour sweet by feeling the different shapes.

3012.belief: When finding the probability of an outcome based on a frequency table, pupils may use the number of different categories as the denominator rather than the total frequency.
3012.statement: When finding the probability of an outcome based on a frequency table, pupils may use the number of different categories as the denominator rather than the total frequency.
3012.correction: When strawberry flavoured sweets have a frequency of 11, it means that 11 of the sweets in the box are strawberry flavoured. The box of sweets could be visually represented with each sweet being shown by the first letter of its flavour.

5823.belief: A probability tree can only have two branches.
5823.statement: A probability tree can only have two branches.
5823.correction: A probability tree can have any number of branches on a layer, but the more branches you want to include, the trickier and less practical the probability tree is to draw and use.

6336.statement: Pupils may count the number of outcomes and state this as the probability.
6336.correction: Remind pupils that the probability scale is between 0 and 1, so an answer of 3 is not correct.

10798.belief: Venn diagrams are useful when generating a complete list of outcomes and showing the probabilities of that list.
10798.statement: Venn diagrams are useful when generating a complete list of outcomes and showing the probabilities of that list.
10798.correction: Venn diagrams can be very useful when categorising already known outcomes into events. The Venn diagram can then be used to calculate probabilities. However, Venn diagrams are not as useful when generating a list of outcomes.

6730.statement: Pupils may over generalise and think that the sum of all possible events sum to 1. E.g. when rolling a standard six-sided dice, P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6) = 1.
6730.correction: Emphasise that probabilities sum to 1 when the events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. E.g. in the calculation P(multiple of 6) + P(factor of 6), the outcome '6' is counted twice.

7370.statement: Pupils may struggle with finding the probability of A or B, and may count the outcomes that belong to A and B twice.
7370.correction: If you use an example, such as visiting particular countries, ask the pupils how someone would respond to the question 'have you visited X or Y' if they have in fact visited both countries.

9167.belief: When I see a probability tree, I always multiply the probabilities.
9167.statement: When I see a probability tree, I always multiply the probabilities.
9167.correction: If a probability tree shows a two-stage trial, then the probability of an outcome is the product of the probabilities of the outcomes at each stage. The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of each outcome in the event.

5822.belief: The probability of an event is the product of the probability of each outcome in the event.
5822.statement: The probability of an event is the product of the probability of each outcome in the event.
5822.correction: The probability of an event is the sum of the probability of each outcome in the event seen in the sample space of a diagram. For example, in the sample space at the end of a probability tree, or by adding the outcomes in the sample space of a table.

3727.belief: When increasing a probability by 50%, pupils may choose to add 50% onto the existing probability rather than multiplying by 1.5.
3727.statement: When increasing a probability by 50%, pupils may choose to add 50% onto the existing probability rather than multiplying by 1.5.
3727.correction: Make links to any previous work pupils may have done on increasing by a percentage and emphasise that a percentage increase is being applied to the probability.

5999.belief: A sequence is arithmetic and only check the first few terms.
5999.statement: Pupils assume a sequence is arithmetic and only check the first few terms.
5999.correction: Encourage pupils to check all the terms of a sequence they are given to check that the pattern they think they have spotted is continuing.

4643.belief: Misinterpreting the values in an expression for the n^th term. For example, given the n^th term $$3n-5$$ pupils may think that this relates to a sequence that is decreasing by 5 each time.
4643.statement: Misinterpreting the values in an expression for the n^th term. For example, given the n^th term $$3n-5$$ pupils may think that this relates to a sequence that is decreasing by 5 each time
4643.correction: Remind students about how the expression for the n^th term relates to multiples of a number (times tables) and then a shift. For example, 4, 9, 14, 19,... can be seen as the 5 times table shifted down 1.

594.belief: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
594.statement: After becoming very familiar with arithmetic sequences pupils can find the difference between the first two terms and just assume the sequence is arithmetic.
594.correction: Explore a large number of geometric and arithmetic sequences and see if pupils can articulate how they check if a sequence is geometric. They might say the terms of the sequence grow more quickly (for some geometric sequences).

7585.statement: Pupils may thing that given the graph is continuous, the sequence can contain all of the values represented by the line.
7585.correction: It is important that pupils know when it is appropriate to draw a line to graph sequences and whether values on the line have any meaning. Sequences are often given as a list of terms and without context we cannot assume the sequence is continuous.

9577.belief: Square numbers are any number that can be squared.
9577.statement: Square numbers are any number that can be squared.
9577.correction: Give students counters or let them draw dot patterns to explore square numbers geometrically as well as numerically.

7870.belief: Given a graph is continuous, the sequence can contain all of the values represented by the line.
7870.statement: Pupils may think that given a graph is continuous, the sequence can contain all of the values represented by the line.
7870.correction: It is important that pupils know when it is appropriate to draw a line to graph sequences and whether values on the line have any meaning. Sequences are often given as a list of terms and without context we cannot assume the sequence is continuous.

9214.belief: Sequences are either arithmetic or geometric.
9214.statement: Sequences are either arithmetic or geometric.
9214.correction: There are many ways sequences can be generated and you can usually find more than one rule than can fit the first few terms of a sequence. Exploring these will ensure pupils don't have a narrow experience of sequences.

1770.belief: If you combine two sequences of the same type the resulting sequence will still be that type.
1770.statement: If you combine two sequences of the same type the resulting sequence will still be that type.
1770.correction: Adding corresponding terms of two sequences will be good preparation for future units but it also a way to explore what sequences can be generated by combining other sequences.

6708.statement: Pupils forget to multiply every term in the bracket by the term outside the bracket.
6708.correction: Remind pupils about the distributive law with numerical examples, e.g. 4(3 + 7) and show that this is not equivalent to 12 + 7. Using algebra tiles can also help pupils to make sense of this skill.

2717.belief: If equations contain brackets you always need to expand them before solving.
2717.statement: If equations contain brackets you always need to expand them before solving.
2717.correction: Try to encourage pupils to use their factors and multiples knowledge to decide if it is more efficient to expand first or not.

4649.correction: Relating back to numerical examples and showing that 12 × 34 is not just 10 × 30 + 2 × 4. Using algebra tiles and area models can help to support student's understanding.

9578.belief: Squaring a binomial is the same as just squaring each term. This can then cause confusion with difference of two squares where expanding a pair of binomials does result in just two terms.
9578.statement: Squaring a binomial is the same as just squaring each term. This can then cause confusion with difference of two squares where expanding a pair of binomials does result in just two terms.
9578.correction: Using an area model and taking time to check the partial products each time, particularly with negative terms, should help students to check if they have expanded correctly.

4664.belief: Mistakes with partial products are even more common where algebraic terms in the binomials have coefficients greater than 1. It is common to find pupils writing that the product of 2x and 3x is 5x.
4664.statement: Mistakes with partial products are even more common where algebraic terms in the binomials have coefficients greater than 1. It is common to find pupils writing that the product of 2x and 3x is 5x
4664.correction: Reminding pupils that because multiplication is commutative the product of 2x and 3x can be thought of as 2 × 3 × x × x

8783.belief: Rearranging equations means you can just swap where terms are.
8783.statement: Rearranging equations means you can just swap where terms are.
8783.correction: Remind pupils that subtraction and division are not commutative so swapping the order will matter.

8758.belief: Rather than learning to rearrange multiplicative relationships pupils can just learn the rearrangements or use a trick.
8758.statement: Rather than learning to rearrange multiplicative relationships pupils can just learn the rearrangements or use a trick.
8758.correction: There are many situations in school and out where this skill is valuable and understanding how to manipulate these relationships will help pupils to understand the mathematics rather than just learn a set of procedures or lots of formulae.

10000.belief: The subject of a formula is just the first term in the formula.
10000.statement: The subject of a formula is just the first term in the formula.
10000.correction: Draw attention to the variety of equations and formulae used in the lesson.

3365.belief: The gradient of a line given the equation of the line is always just the coefficient of the x term.
3365.statement: That the gradient of a line given the equation of the line is always just the coefficient of the x term.
3365.correction: Using graphing software to explore this could help.

939.belief: Changing the subject of an equation or formula is only done when you are told to.
939.statement: Changing the subject of an equation or formula is only done when you are told to.
939.correction: Having students practise rearranging before substituting and vice versa allows them to decide when the skill could be useful.

10027.belief: When subtracting expression pupils forget to subtract both terms from the second espression.
10027.statement: When subtracting expression pupils forget to subtract both terms from the second espression.
10027.correction: Watch out for mistakes with negatives here. Pupils should find it much easier to re-write subtractions as additions of additive inverses and that way they only need to add.

4872.belief: You need to know all the lengths or all of the angles in a pair of triangles to know that they are similar.
4872.statement: You need to know all the lengths or all of the angles in a pair of triangles to know that they are similar.
4872.correction: Remind pupils that they do not necessarily need to know all of the length and angles to determine whether two triangles are congruent, so they don't all need to be known to determine similarity.

6636.statement: Pupils may find it initially difficult to see how Pythagoras' theorem can be used when a right-angled triangle is not immediately available.
6636.correction: Encourage pupils to draw their own diagram in cases where there is not one provided. In cases where pairs of coordinates are being used, encourage pupils to draw on horizontal and vertical line segments.

8778.belief: When reading the values of the trigonometric functions during the explanation slides and the tasks, pupils may think that all the values taken from the graphs are fully accurate.
8778.statement: When reading the values of the trigonometric functions during the explanation slides and the tasks, pupils may think that all the values taken from the graphs are fully accurate.
8778.correction: Explain that many of the values from the trigonometric functions have digits beyond the second decimal place. However, two decimal places is a reasonable degree of accuracy for reading values from the graphs during this lesson.

9304.correction: The values of the sine or cosine of an angle do not scale linearly. We can see from the unit circle that an angle of 30° meets the circle at a height of 0.5 units, whilst an angle of 60° meets the circle at a height of approximately 0.87 units.

10141.correction: The values of tan of an angle do not scale linearly. From the unit circle, we see that an angle of 30° meets a tangent to the circle at a height of approx. 0.58 units, whilst an angle of 60° meets the same tangent at a height of approx. 1.73 units.

9309.belief: The sine formula is only used to find the length of a side opposite an angle.
9309.statement: The sine formula is only used to find the length of a side opposite an angle.
9309.correction: Whilst the sine formula can be used to find the length of a side opposite an angle, a rearrangement of the formula also allows us to find the length of the hypotenuse given the opposite side. The arcsine function allows us to find the angle, itself.

2056.belief: The cosine formula is only used to find the length of a side adjacent to an angle.
2056.statement: The cosine formula is only used to find the length of a side adjacent to an angle.
2056.correction: The cosine formula can be used to find the length of a side adjacent to an angle. A rearrangement of the formula also allows us to find the length of the hypotenuse given the adjacent side. The arccosine function allows us to find the angle, itself.

6750.statement: Pupils may get the fraction (opposite/adjacent) inverted and this will still return an answer so they may believe they are correct.
6750.correction: Remind pupils to sense check their answers. The larger the angle, the longer the opposite side will be.

6082.belief: The horizontal edge of the triangle is always the adjacent.
6082.statement: Pupils may believe the horizontal edge of the triangle is always the adjacent.
6082.correction: Emphasise that the labelling of the triangle is based around the focus angle and use right-angled triangles with various orientations.

7366.statement: Pupils may struggle to find a right-angled triangle within the context of the question.
7366.correction: Encourage the pupils to sketch the question and consider adding a perpendicular line to the diagram.

7405.statement: Pupils may struggle to identify a right-angled triangle in the problem.
7405.correction: Encourage pupils to sketch the question out and add any known right angles or perpendicular lines, as this may lead to a right-angled triangle.

4448.belief: There are many ways to multiply decimals or large numbers. With decimals, some pupils choose to multiply decimals using the column method and incorrectly use a decimal point when calculating answers.
4448.statement: There are many ways to multiply decimals or large numbers. With decimals, some pupils choose to multiply decimals using the column method and incorrectly use a decimal point when calculating answers.
4448.correction: When multiplying decimals, converting the calculation using integers and powers of 10 makes the calculation easier to work with.

10577.belief: Use of addition instead of multiplication when finding factors.
10577.statement: Use of addition instead of multiplication when finding factors.
10577.correction: Reiterate that the product of prime factors is unique.

4911.belief: A negative exponent implies that the entire value is negative.
4911.statement: A negative exponent implies that the entire value is negative.
4911.correction: Refer back to the table showing the structure of how the negative exponents occur and highlight that none of the decimal values are negative.

6822.statement: Pupils can incorrectly write a number in standard form or use a number in incorrect standard form whereby the number A does not satisfy 1 ≤ A < 10 or pupils use division of positive powers of 10.
6822.correction: Standard form represents a multiplicative relationship, so there should always be a multiplication. Embedding the understanding that negative exponents refer to 1/10^n is important. Using the place value chart with fractional and exponent form helps.

9212.belief: All sequences have to be arithmetic (linear) or geometric.
9212.statement: All sequences have to be arithmetic (linear) or geometric.
9212.correction: There are many types of sequences; arithmetic and geometric are just two types.

9215.belief: All sequences can go on infinitely.
9215.statement: All sequences can go on infinitely.
9215.correction: When we think abstractly and start a sequence such as 8, 10, 12, 14, 16,... it is possible that it goes on infinitely. However, if we applied this sequence to a context such as pairs of pupils getting on a bus, then a physical limit will apply.

5605.belief: After plotting the integer coordinate pairs of a quadratic, they should be joined with a straight line.
5605.statement: After plotting the integer coordinate pairs of a quadratic, they should be joined with a straight line.
5605.correction: Use graphing technology to plot coordinate pairs that use smaller and smaller non-integer steps between $$x$$-coordinates. This will reveal the true, curved nature of the line.

2756.belief: Estimation and approximation are only required skills when working solely with number problems.
2756.statement: Estimation and approximation are only required skills when working solely with number problems.
2756.correction: In problem solving it can be really useful to sketch an approximation of a certain graph such as a linear equation. Seeing where the $$y$$-intercept is and drawing an approximate gradient could help us identify solutions.

10112.belief: A table of values should always be filled in and all points plotted in order to graph a linear equation.
10112.statement: A table of values should always be filled in and all points plotted in order to graph a linear equation.
10112.correction: A linear equation will form a straight line graph therefore we only need to know two points in order to draw the line.

9307.belief: Since linear equations (typically) have one solution, all equations have one solution.
9307.statement: Since linear equations (typically) have one solution, all equations have one solution.
9307.correction: Ask pupils to compare the graphical solution to a linear equation with the graphical solution to a quadratic equation. This will enable them to see that it is possible for a quadratic equation to have more than one solution.

4200.belief: The line on a distance time graph can go in any direction.
4200.statement: The line on a distance time graph can go in any direction.
4200.correction: The line may be horizontal, time changing without a change in distance, but it can not be vertical. That would be a change in distance without a change in time. Additionally, our line cannot go backwards; time is always moving forwards.

5196.belief: There is only one way to solve linear equations; by manipulation and isolating the variable(s).
5196.statement: There is only one way to solve linear equations; by manipulation and isolating the variable(s).
5196.correction: When we plot more than one linear equation on a graph we can use the intersection to find the solution.

2421.belief: A distance time graph will always be constructed with straight lines.
2421.statement: A distance time graph will always be constructed with straight lines.
2421.correction: A straight line represents a consistent rate of a change, a consistent speed. In reality we need to model acceleration and deceleration which will involve curved lines.

796.belief: When calculating the amount of electricity produced by a solar panel, pupils may forget to convert its power rating from watts to kilowatts.
796.statement: When calculating the amount of electricity produced by a solar panel, pupils may forget to convert its power rating from watts to kilowatts.
796.correction: Always check whether the units for any values given in the informatin match the units that are required for the formula.

797.belief: When calculating the amount of emissions per mile, pupils may forget to convert the information given from grams to kilograms.
797.statement: When calculating the amount of emissions per mile, pupils may forget to convert the information given from grams to kilograms.
797.correction: Always check whether the units for any values given in the information match the units that are required for the formula.

5950.statement: Pupils may add together costs that are expressed in different units (e.g. the cost of petrol in pence and the cost of a car park in pounds) without considering the implications on place value.
5950.correction: Writing units on your answers to each stage of working can help you to double check whether numbers in subsequent calculations are expressed in the same units.

10171.belief: The temperature tells us how hot it will feel.
10171.statement: The temperature tells us how hot it will feel.
10171.correction: The temperature given in a weather report is normally the air temperature. The 'feel like' temperature may be different depending on multiple factors.

10963.belief: If the weather report has the rain icon, it means it will rain.
10963.statement: If the weather report has the rain icon, it means it will rain.
10963.correction: The rain symbol is to denote what type of rain it is likely to be should it rain. The percentage chance of rain then informs us about how likely it is to rain.

1849.belief: When comparing the modal class for two datasets, pupils may think that the dataset with the greatest modal class is the one which has the greatest frequency for its modal class.
1849.statement: When comparing the modal class for two datasets, pupils may think that the dataset with the greatest modal class is the one which has the greatest frequency for its modal class
1849.correction: Use the frequency to identify the modal class for each dataset, but then compare the values within each class to determine which dataset has the greatest modal class.

5164.belief: One trend line appearing higher on a graph than a different trend line means the higher line shows more change over time.
5164.statement: One trend line appearing higher on a graph than a different trend line means the higher line shows more change over time.
5164.correction: It is the gradient of a trend line that informs how quickly something is changing with respect to time.

10554.belief: An urban area should implement all of the strategies to make itself greener.
10554.statement: An urban area should implement all of the strategies to make itself greener.
10554.correction: Not all strategies are viable for every urban area and some will be more effective than others depending on the location.

5458.belief: When performing divisions to calculate the maximum number of plants that fit into a space, pupils may round decimal answers up to the nearest integer (e.g. round 4.5 plants up to 5 plants).
5458.statement: When performing divisions to calculate the maximum number of plants that fit into a space, pupils may round decimal answers up to the nearest integer (e.g. round 4.5 plants up to 5 plants).
5458.correction: The context would suggest that it may be more appropriate to truncate decimal answers to an integer rather than rounding them up to the nearest integer (e.g. there is not enough space available to fit the 5th plant).

2902.belief: The factors mentioned in the lesson are the only factors to consider when considering costs/profits of livestock.
2902.statement: The factors mentioned in the lesson are the only factors to consider when considering costs/profits of livestock.
2902.correction: There are many more factors to consider. Pupils could research these or brainstorm with a partner. An example could be selling the wool from any sheep owned.

1937.correction: Pupils may benefit from having two lists of metric and imperial measures to reference should they need to.

6327.statement: Pupils may not be convinced that a right angled triangle is formed.
6327.correction: For the model, we assume that the terrain feature is perpendicular to the surface.

7993.belief: The mathematical conventions for rounding should apply.
7993.statement: Pupils may think the mathematical conventions for rounding should apply.
7993.correction: This is rounding in a practical context and pupils should consider what the effects of rounding up and down are and how they affect the answer.

7546.correction: Each variable in a formula represents something. Substituting for one variable at a time may help ensure that values are in the correct places.

6994.statement: Pupils mix-up the sides of the right-angled triangle when using Pythagoras' theorem.
6994.correction: Pupils may benefit from labelling the right-angled triangle so that the hypotenuse is clearly identified.

7742.belief: The cost per hour can be reduced if less than an hour is required (venue hire).
7742.statement: Pupils may think the cost per hour can be reduced if less than an hour is required (venue hire).
7742.correction: This may be possible but should not be assumed when costing for an event as otherwise this could lead to a loss rather than a profit. If unknown, assume not.

8475.statement: Pupils may be uncertain as to whether an image has rotational symmetry.
8475.correction: Tracing paper may be useful here. Pupils can trace the image and then rotate the tracing paper to determine if an image has rotational symmetry.

9021.belief: Rounding incorrectly for the stated context.
9021.statement: Rounding incorrectly for the stated context.
9021.correction: Pupils should consider the situation and ask - if rounding down, will there be enough? If rounding up, does this cover all cases? Thinking about the situation and trying different values to see what works can also help.

7371.statement: Pupils may struggle in the first learning cycle with where each object should be placed.
7371.correction: The closer to the observation point an object is, the larger it appears to be. So if we want an object to appear larger than something else, we need to place it closer to the camera.

10020.belief: Substituting the wrong values into the formulas.
10020.statement: Substituting the wrong values into the formulas.
10020.correction: The formulas are written in words so ensure pupils check that what they are substituting is the correct value by rereading the description for each value.

6308.statement: Pupils may not consider the maximum of the 'bins' in learning cycle 1.
6308.correction: It can be helpful for pupils to have a running total for the values assigned to each 'bin' so that they know when it is full and no more values can be assigned there.

8530.statement: Pupils may be unfamiliar with train timetables and how to interpret them.
8530.correction: Each column of times can be given a header of Train 1, Train 2 etc. This will make it clearer that the times in a column refer to when that train will reach a station.

7499.statement: Pupils may struggle with the 'and' statements in the logic part of the lesson.
7499.correction: For the statement to be true, the whole statement must be true. This refers to both clauses that are joined by the word 'and'. If even one of the clauses is not true, then the entire statement can be declared not true (even if one clause is true).

6297.statement: Pupils may be confused about whether to multiply or divide when dealing with reversing percentage change.
6297.correction: The first learning cycle addresses this and you may wish to display the example on a whiteboard for the entire lesson for pupils to refer to.

8814.belief: Reducing the cost to increase sales is always the best option.
8814.statement: Reducing the cost to increase sales is always the best option.
8814.correction: Although this may seem a good idea, increasing the number of units sold means increasing the amount made and therefore the cost to the business. Therefore the situation needs to be carefully considered.

7917.belief: Improvement comes from choosing the maximum options for training straight away.
7917.statement: Pupils may think that improvement comes from choosing the maximum options for training straight away.
7917.correction: In order to protect the body and give it time to adjust/grow, coaches will gradually increase the intensity of a training programme. This helps to prevent injury to the athlete.

7781.belief: Drawing a graph with a broken axis is incorrect.
7781.statement: Pupils may think that drawing a graph with a broken axis is incorrect.
7781.correction: It is fine to do this (and is sometimes necessary) but it is important to acknowledge this when trying to draw conclusions from the graph.

7660.belief: It is always best to buy a 'deal' as deals are always a good thing.
7660.statement: Pupils may think that it is always best to buy a 'deal' as deals are always a good thing.
7660.correction: Throughout the lesson it is demonstrated that a deal or promotion may not always be right for every customer. Is a deal worth it if you don't need to buy that much?

11027.belief: Winning an election means receiving over half the vote.
11027.statement: Winning an election means receiving over half the vote.
11027.correction: Under the First Past the Post system, a winning candidate must receive more votes than any other candidate. This may not mean receiving over half of the total vote.

4680.belief: Mixing up STV and AV as both involve ranking candidates from favourite to least.
4680.statement: Mixing up STV and AV as both involve ranking candidates from favourite to least.
4680.correction: With STV, excess votes from the winning candidates are also reassigned.

10123.belief: Taking 20% off an amount after a percentage change will result in the original amount before 20% was added.
10123.statement: Taking 20% off an amount after a percentage change will result in the original amount before 20% was added.
10123.correction: These are percentages of different amounts so, given that we are calculating 20% in both cases, this will not work.

807.belief: Calculators can only be used to add, subtract, multiply or divide.
807.statement: Calculators can only be used to add, subtract, multiply or divide.
807.correction: They can be used to perform basic calculations but they can also do so much more.

3450.belief: It can be hard to spot like terms where there are multiple variables with exponents. Therefore opportunities to simplify by collecting like terms can be missed.
3450.statement: It can be hard to spot like terms where there are multiple variables with exponents. Therefore opportunities to simplify by collecting like terms can be missed.
3450.correction: When multiplying variables together, write the variables in alphabetical order. This will make it easier to identify like terms.

3700.belief: Incorrect evaluation of expressions is common when negative values are substituted. Especially where negative values are squared or pupils rely on calculators without being confident of their use.
3700.statement: Incorrect evaluation of expressions is common when negative values are substituted. Especially where negative values are squared or pupils rely on calculators without being confident of their use.
3700.correction: When substituting, always put brackets around the value which is substituted. This helps avoid mistakes when using a calculator as well.

7851.belief: The formula for the number of days in a week is w=7d because a week has seven days.
7851.statement: Pupils can think the formula for the number of days in a week is w=7d because a week has seven days.
7851.correction: Pupils should always write down exactly what the letter is representing. E.g. 'the number of days' and 'the number of weeks'. Then think about what calculation they are doing. 'To find the number of days I multiply the number of weeks by 7'. d=7w.

6651.statement: Pupils find simplifying expressions which are the difference of two bracketed expressions difficult.
6651.correction: There are two equivalent methods detailed in learning cycle two. Spend time on both, getting pupils to explore their equivalence. If pupils are struggling, considering subtraction as adding the negative value is the easiest to model.

4088.belief: Leaving answers which are not fully factorised when they are required to.
4088.statement: Leaving answers which are not fully factorised when they are required to.
4088.correction: There should be a focus on reading questions to decipher what they are being asked to do. When they have to fully factorise they need the highest common factor of all the terms. LC3 focuses on situations where they are not going to fully factorise.

3128.belief: When forming expressions brackets can be missed out or incorrectly used.
3128.statement: When forming expressions brackets can be missed out or incorrectly used.
3128.correction: Review priority of operations. Testing algebraic manipulations with numerical values can be useful when pupils are unsure if things are equivalent. E.g. the difference between 2(x + 4) and 2x + 4 can be shown with 2(5 + 4) and 2(5) + 4

4206.belief: If a linear equation involves brackets, these always have to be expanded first.
4206.statement: If a linear equation involves brackets, these always have to be expanded first.
4206.correction: Get pupils to use knowledge of factors and collecting like terms to simplify problems.

8784.belief: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'.
8784.statement: When rearranging multiplicative relationships, the values just 'swap'.
8784.correction: Pupils should understand how to manipulate multiplicative relationships properly instead of relying on a 'trick'. This will be useful in other subject areas as well.

6757.statement: Pupils often get signs the incorrect way round in the binomials. E.g. (x+2)(x-4) instead of (x-2)(x+4)
6757.correction: Encourage pupils to always expand their binomials to check they are correct. Using representations such as an area model should reduce the likelihood of this as pupils focus on the structure and reason behind their choices.

5105.belief: Once shown the difference of two squares, pupils may think that squaring each term in a binomial is the correct way to expand binomials such as (x+3)^2.
5105.statement: Once shown the difference of two squares, pupils may think that squaring each term in a binomial is the correct way to expand binomials such as (x+3)^2
5105.correction: Spend time investigating where the difference of two squares occurs, use representations such as algebra tiles and area models.

9414.belief: The solutions are just the constants in the binomials.
9414.statement: That the solutions are just the constants in the binomials.
9414.correction: After factorising, pupils should be writing the one step equations, equal to zero, before writing the solutions.

3694.belief: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
3694.statement: Including solutions which are not valid in the context of the question.
3694.correction: Pupils should finish every problem by substituting their solutions back into the original problem. This will help them check their answers but also make them think about whether their solutions are valid in context.

10019.correction: Putting brackets around all substituted values is good practice.

3712.belief: Incorrectly identifying when simultaneous equations can be formed. This can lead to pupils using the same letter in two equations to represent different things.
3712.statement: Incorrectly identifying when simultaneous equations can be formed. This can lead to pupils using the same letter in two equations to represent different things.
3712.correction: Pupils should be writing down precisely what the variable represent in context. They can then compare whether they are using the same letter to represent the same thing in two different equations.

4661.belief: Mistakes can be made when subtracting negative values. E.g. thinking that 5 - - 2 = 3.
4661.statement: Mistakes can be made when subtracting negative values. E.g. thinking that 5 - - 2 = 3.
4661.correction: Consider additive inverses, subtracting a negative is the same as adding the additive inverse. Pupils should be able to spot mistakes in learning cycle 1 by checking their new equation is still true.

10029.belief: Subtracting the variables one way round but the constants the other way.
10029.statement: Subtracting the variables one way round but the constants the other way.
10029.correction: Pupils could rewrite their equations so the one they are subtracting is underneath in a column method. For this lesson, the answers are in context so pupils should spot when negative answers do not make sense.

5457.belief: Performing different operations on different variables. E.g. subtracting one variable to eliminate then adding the other variable and constant. Pupils incorrectly think they are adding to eliminate.
5457.statement: Performing different operations on different variables. E.g. subtracting one variable to eliminate then adding the other variable and constant. Pupils incorrectly think they are adding to eliminate.
5457.correction: This is caused by negative number skills. Subtracting two identical values always gives zero even if both are negative. If a term is the same in both equations, we subtract to eliminate. Clear working is crucial here.

3100.belief: Forgetting to multiply every term in the equation when scaling or not multiplying every term by the same value.
3100.statement: Forgetting to multiply every term in the equation when scaling or not multiplying every term by the same value.
3100.correction: Remind pupils that in order to maintain equality, the entire expression on both sides of the equals sign must be multiplied by the same value. Clear working and checking solutions can help pupils spot when they have made this mistake.

3711.belief: Incorrectly expanding brackets or not using brackets when one expression is substituted into another.
3711.statement: Incorrectly expanding brackets or not using brackets when one expression is substituted into another.
3711.correction: Pupils should always use brackets when substituting. Remind them of the distributive law and that multiplying a negative value by a negative value gives a positive value. Checking final answers should catch these mistakes.

2719.correction: Some equations have one solution but, some have no solutions, some have two solutions, some have more than two solutions.

5143.belief: One method is superior when solving simultaneous equations.
5143.statement: One method is superior when solving simultaneous equations.
5143.correction: Understanding that there are often multiple ways to solve the same problem and then be able to accurately execute a variety of methods is very useful. In this topic, it can enable pupils to confirm their solutions.

9303.belief: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
9303.statement: Simultaneous equations cannot be applied usefully to real-world scenarios.
9303.correction: The skill of solving a pair of simultaneous equations can be applied to a wide variety of problems and provides us with answers in a wide variety of contexts.

10714.belief: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease.
10714.statement: When using multipliers, pupils can mistake a decimal for the percentage decrease. e.g. 0.52 is a 52% decrease, rather than recognising a 48% decrease
10714.correction: Reminding students that a decimal multiplier greater than 1 means an increase, and a decimal multiplier less than 1 means a decrease. The latter requires a subtraction from 1 or 100%

7069.statement: Pupils should pay careful attention to what the question asks. Working out the overall amount after a simple or compound increase is different to working out the total interest only.
7069.correction: Pupils can underline or highlight the key instruction to the question e.g. Total amount or total interest, to remind them of the need to subtract from the original amount or not.

2908.belief: Failing to understand the difference between simple and compound interest. And, therefore finding the interest for one time period and multiplying it by the number of time periods.
2908.statement: Failing to understand the difference between simple and compound interest. And, therefore finding the interest for one time period and multiplying it by the number of time periods.
2908.correction: Pupils can forget to transfer the year end balance as the starting balance of the next year. Using repeated language can help. E.g. "At the end of year 2 there was... in the account, so, at the beginning of year 3 there was... in the account."

470.belief: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
470.statement: Assuming that an increase of 10% followed by a decrease of 10% takes you back to 100%, etc.
470.correction: Provide plenty of examples to illustrate the structure of what happens. If you increase a number by a percentage the number will increase meaning that you will be finding 10% of a larger number and hence decrease by more.

5241.belief: When ordering decimals, the more significant figures the greater the number.
5241.statement: When ordering decimals, the more significant figures the greater the number.
5241.correction: When ordering decimals, having the same number of decimal places allows the pupils to see the magnitude of the number more clearly.

3702.belief: The incorrect input of a mixed number is common i.e some pupils press a number then the fraction button. Others inefficiently sum the integer and proper fraction.
3702.statement: The incorrect input of a mixed number is common i.e some pupils press a number then the fraction button. Others inefficiently sum the integer and proper fraction.
3702.correction: Reiterating the mixed number button is located above the proper fraction button.

5021.belief: Any number is a square or cube number because it can be squared or cubed.
5021.statement: Any number is a square or cube number because it can be squared or cubed.
5021.correction: A square number is the result of a number being multiplied by itself. Emphasis must be on the result. A cube number is a number that has been multiplied by itself three times. Emphasis must be on the result of the repeated multiplication.

4758.belief: When multiplying terms with coefficients, pupils also add the coefficients as well as the exponents.
4758.statement: When multiplying terms with coefficients, pupils also add the coefficients as well as the exponents.
4758.correction: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression using the associative and commutative laws, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped. This hopefully avoids this error as they can see it is the product of the numbers.

2432.belief: When dividing terms with coefficients, pupils also subtract the coefficients as well as the exponents.
2432.statement: When dividing terms with coefficients, pupils also subtract the coefficients as well as the exponents.
2432.correction: Pupils should be encouraged to rewrite their expression as a fraction, with the number parts grouped and powers grouped. This hopefully avoids this error as they can see the fraction line as a division.

3102.belief: Forgetting to raise the coefficient to the power as well as the power term.
3102.statement: Forgetting to raise the coefficient to the power as well as the power term.
3102.correction: Highlight that everything in the bracket is being affected by the power. By showing examples where the bracket is written in expanded form and then the repeated multiplication helps with this.

5014.belief: Any number with an index of 0 equates to 0.
5014.statement: Any number with an index of 0 equates to 0
5014.correction: Reiterate the division of any number by itself is 1. This applies with laws of indices too. E.g 8^4 / 8^4 = 8^0. Any number divided by itself gives 1, therefore 8^0 = 1. For more advanced understanding, algebraic can be used instead of numbers.

10707.belief: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
10707.statement: Using the laws of indices, when dividing by a number with a negative exponent pupils can incorrectly subtract the negative exponent.
10707.correction: When the bases of all the numbers are the same, forming an equation with the exponents can reduce errors.

5019.belief: When a number is not quite written in standard form, pupils can incorrectly convert the number.
5019.statement: When a number is not quite written in standard form, pupils can incorrectly convert the number.
5019.correction: When the A number is greater than 10, add the necessary multiplications of 10 to the index of 10. When the A number is less than 10, subtract the necessary multiplications of 10 from the index of 10.

118.belief: When adding numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
118.statement: When adding numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
118.correction: The use of the place value chart shows how the magnitude does not change to the sum of the powers of 10. The place value chart can support pupils to make the correct addition or subtraction of large or small numbers.

10028.belief: When subtracting numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
10028.statement: When subtracting numbers in standard form, pupils can also add the exponents of 10.
10028.correction: The use of the place value chart shows how the magnitude does not change to the sum of the powers of 10. The place value chart can support pupils to make the correct addition or subtraction of large or small numbers.

2431.belief: When the dividing numbers written in standard form changing the multiplication symbol between the number and power of ten to a division symbol.
2431.statement: When the dividing numbers written in standard form changing the multiplication symbol between the number and power of ten to a division symbol.
2431.correction: Encourage pupils to write any division as a fraction. This makes the maintenance of the multiplication symbol easier to see.

3705.belief: Incorrect use of the calculator when finding the mean of numbers. Omitting the brackets when summing the values.
3705.statement: Incorrect use of the calculator when finding the mean of numbers. Omitting the brackets when summing the values.
3705.correction: Encourage pupils to calculate the sum of the values and record this before dividing by the number of values. This also encourages a record of a method.

10062.belief: Surds are any number with a root symbol.
10062.statement: Surds are any number with a root symbol.
10062.correction: √4 is not a surd as it is equivalent to 2.

6098.belief: As mean, median and mode are all averages that they are all as useful as each other for every data set.
6098.statement: Pupils may believe that as mean, median and mode are all averages that they are all as useful as each other for every data set.
6098.correction: Using non qualitative data to show that the mean and median cannot be calculated, so the mode would be the only option. Showing data sets that have the same mean value but are considerably different to each other.

7102.statement: Pupils may reach false conclusions by not following the Statistical Enquiry Cycle and skipping stages.
7102.correction: Ask pupils to consider trying to draw conclusions from a large data set of raw values, where no processing or representation has taken place, to highlight the need for that stage in particular.

8173.belief: Primary data means data they collect first hand (and no one else can collect it).
8173.statement: Pupils may think that primary data means data they collect first hand (and no one else can collect it).
8173.correction: Primary data refers to data that are directly collected for specific use in an investigation. This means that a team of researchers could collect the data for you for your investigation and this is still primary data.

4810.belief: Names in a hat is the simplest way to perform a simple random sample.
4810.statement: Names in a hat is the simplest way to perform a simple random sample.
4810.correction: This can be true for very small populations but becomes time consuming quickly.

9083.belief: Samples always represent the population from which they are drawn as they come from that population.
9083.statement: Samples always represent the population from which they are drawn as they come from that population.
9083.correction: Taking multiple large samples allows us to begin to generalise the results to the whole population.

7544.statement: Pupils may struggle to write response boxes that do not overlap for continuous data.
7544.correction: Remind pupils of how to write intervals using inequality symbols.

8531.statement: Pupils may unintentionally add bias to their questions.
8531.correction: Have other pupils check questions for any bias and support their peers in rewording them.

651.correction: A biased sample is sometimes useful if the sample is proportional to the population and/or it focuses on a section of the population relevant to the investigation.

8474.statement: Pupils may be uncertain about which variable to plot on the horizontal axis if they are unsure about which is the independent variable and which is the dependent variable.
