8474.correction: Getting it wrong should not affect your interpretations of the data too much and sometimes neither variable might be dependent on the other. If you are unsure, consider which variable seems the most likely to be affecting the other in context.

2055.belief: Correlation between two variables always means that one variable has a causal effect on the other.
2055.statement: Correlation between two variables always means that one variable has a causal effect on the other.
2055.correction: Two variables may have correlation because they are both dependent on a third variable. E.g. one slide shows correlation between the number of cell towers in a region and the amount of transport emissions, which both correlate with population.

4198.belief: The line of best fit always start at the origin.
4198.statement: The line of best fit always start at the origin.
4198.correction: The line of best fit could start at the origin but it does not always start there. This could be exemplified clearly with a scatter graph that has negative correlation.

3836.belief: Interpolation and extrapolation always produce accurate predictions.
3836.statement: Interpolation and extrapolation always produce accurate predictions.
3836.correction: Extrapolation may not be valid as this is outside the observed set of data values (e.g. a linear trend might not continue indefinitely). Interpolation may not be valid due to the limitations of the data set.

5283.belief: An outlier always has values that are outside the range of the dataset (i.e. at the start or end of a dataset).
5283.statement: An outlier always has values that are outside the range of the dataset (i.e. at the start or end of a dataset).
5283.correction: For bivariate data, a data point may be distinct from the rest of the data because the value of one of its variable is extremely less/greater than other points that have a similar value in its other variable.

10332.belief: Time series graphs always use years as the time interval.
10332.statement: Time series graphs always use years as the time interval.
10332.correction: The time interval used in a time series graph depends on what the graph is intended to show.

7081.statement: Pupils may place too much confidence in the accuracy of predictions based on extrapolating time series graphs into the future.
7081.correction: While extrapolating a time series graph provide an indication of what future results may be, predictions are not guaranteed. Context should also be considered in these cases (e.g. whether there is a natural limit to how high a variable may reach).

5572.belief: A plausible conclusion or claim must be true when it is presented with data.
5572.statement: A plausible conclusion or claim must be true when it is presented with data.
5572.correction: Graphs can be misinterpreted, which can lead to invalid conclusions.

6709.statement: Pupils may forget to order the data to support finding the median, mode and range.
6709.correction: Use small data (ordered and unordered) to find the range and the median based on position. Race to find range and median of a longer list with one "team" ordering first and the other team not. Ordering can help with speed, accuracy and give insight.

6372.statement: Pupils may divide the total by the number of rows in the frequency table when finding the mean.
6372.correction: On most occasions, the pupils calculated mean will be a value outside of the data set, so a sense-check should highlight that something is not quite right. Encourage pupils to always consider if their answer is reasonable.

3843.belief: The interval widths need to be constant, or conversely that they can be anything.
3843.statement: That the interval widths need to be constant, or conversely that they can be anything.
3843.correction: If interested in people's ages it may be that decades makes sense once over 30 but that significant ages such as 16, 18 and 21 should form boundaries, depending on context. Encourage critical thinking for data with unequal intervals.

2757.correction: Estimation is a process with each step being logical. In this case the estimation is necessary because some of the detail is lost in a grouped frequency table.

9607.belief: The stem always has to have the same number of digits.
9607.statement: That the stem always has to have the same number of digits.
9607.correction: Data with a range between 93 cm and 147 cm, draw the stem-and-leaf diagram but how do they write a key for it? Stress the leaf is the final single digit (all truncated so final digits have same place value), and all other digits form the stem.

2997.belief: You can only find the median class from a stem-and-leaf diagram.
2997.statement: You can only find the median class from a stem-and-leaf diagram.
2997.correction: The data is organised into intervals based on place value. However the full data is still available so the middle value(s) can still be found. The diagram is a form of an ordered list so previous methods for finding the median still apply.

4514.belief: Mean, median and mode are only useful if they are close together.
4514.statement: Mean, median and mode are only useful if they are close together.
4514.correction: If the mean is significantly higher or lower than the other averages, this suggests an extreme value in the data set.

6456.statement: Pupils may feel that one statistical summary is enough to compare two data sets.
6456.correction: Highlight to pupils that the more information you know, the better your understanding of a data set and therefore a more comprehensive comparison can take place. Compare the means of {-120, -100, -50, 0, 1000} and {145, 145, 146, 147, 147}.

6960.statement: Pupils may miss the key in a pictogram, or the axes labels on a bar chart.
6960.correction: Pupils could be provided with a success criteria list, which they get in a habit of checking after constructing pictograms and bar charts.

7104.statement: Pupils may read the frequency or % proportion value off of the y-axis for each group on a composite bar chart.
7104.correction: Remind pupils that another name for composite bar charts is a stacked bar chart and the frequency needs to be calculated.

9570.belief: Spreadsheets should always be used for data analysis as they are perfect.
9570.statement: Spreadsheets should always be used for data analysis as they are perfect.
9570.correction: Spreadsheet software is incredibly powerful but care should be taken as human error can lead to incorrect results.

659.belief: A bigger sector on one pie chart compared to another means a larger frequency.
659.statement: A bigger sector on one pie chart compared to another means a larger frequency.
659.correction: Pie charts show proportion, but tell nothing about frequency. The total frequency of one pie chart could be significantly larger or smaller than the other pie chart.

4691.belief: The mode is the most useful average as it can be calculated from bar charts, pie charts and frequency tables.
4691.statement: The mode is the most useful average as it can be calculated from bar charts, pie charts and frequency tables.
4691.correction: Although it is often the easiest of the averages to calculate, this does not make it the most useful.

1693.belief: Claims can be made based on the data displayed in a chart.
1693.statement: Claims can be made based on the data displayed in a chart.
1693.correction: A claim is only valid for the particular selection of data shown. This can mean that any conclusions are very limited.

2841.belief: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
2841.statement: For example if a measurement of 12 cm has been given to the nearest centimetre assuming the upper bound is 12.4 cm.
2841.correction: Emphasise the infinite nature of a measurement.

9299.belief: Not simplifying the ratio completely or over-simplifying a three part ratio when two of the parts share a further common factor.
9299.statement: Not simplifying the ratio completely or over-simplifying a three part ratio when two of the parts share a further common factor
9299.correction: Link two part ratios back to simplifying fractions and remind pupils to consider if either number is a multiple of 3 as this is often missed. Remind pupils that to simplify a ratio, every part must share the common factor you are dividing by.

3004.belief: Finding the additive relationship between two numbers instead of the multiplicative one.
3004.statement: Finding the additive relationship between two numbers instead of the multiplicative one.
3004.correction: When dealing with any proportional relationships, such as ratios, pupils should be reminded to look for the multiplicative relationship. Using 1 as a middle step can help. e.g. to connect 5 and 8, divide by 5 to make 1 and then multiply by 8.

5827.belief: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
5827.statement: Procedural understanding of sharing in a ratio where pupils add the parts, divide the amount by this and then multiply by each part without considering the information in the question.
5827.correction: In the lesson encourage pupils to look for keywords in the question which indicate if the amount given is the total, one part or the difference. The use of a bar model to display the information can also be used to help pupils.

2037.belief: Converting a ratio e.g. 1: 3 to 1/3 as a fraction.
2037.statement: Converting a ratio e.g. 1: 3 to 1/3 as a fraction.
2037.correction: Drawing out simple ratios using bars can help pupils to see how fractions can correctly be obtained from a given ratio.

2038.belief: Not converting the units correctly in a question or forgetting to have the same units before simplifying a ratio.
2038.statement: Not converting the units correctly in a question or forgetting to have the same units before simplifying a ratio
2038.correction: help pupils to set out ratio tables where they include the units and work through step by step to convert correctly before simplifying. The ratio table can help organise this working.

1772.belief: Combining ratios without using equivalent ratios to equate the common part.
1772.statement: Combining ratios without using equivalent ratios to equate the common part.
1772.correction: Pupils may need to spend extra time finding equivalent ratios and looking at when it is ok to combine ratios or not.

10423.belief: Treating the ratio as the total amount. For example sweets: chocolates in the ratio 6: 7 and 2 chocolates are eaten, thinking the ratio must now be 6: 5.
10423.statement: Treating the ratio as the total amount. For example sweets: chocolates in the ratio 6: 7 and 2 chocolates are eaten, thinking the ratio must now be 6: 5
10423.correction: Looking at how these problems are formed in learning cycle 1 will help and getting pupils to explore how the ratio changes when things are added or removed.

10470.belief: Only two pairs of coordinates are needed to plot a linear graph.
10470.statement: Only two pairs of coordinates are needed to plot a linear graph.
10470.correction: Whilst true, this can cause issues if one pair of coordinates is calculated incorrectly. Encourage pupils to check a third point to ensure they are correct.

6396.statement: Pupils draw x = a as a horizontal line because the x axis is horizontal. Pupils draw y = a as a vertical line because the y axis is vertical.
6396.correction: Consider the points on the line x = 5 and ask pupils to plot 2-3 points. Can they see why it must be a vertical line?

11148.belief: Writing equations of the form y = mx + c and getting the gradient and y-intercept the wrong way round.
11148.statement: Writing equations of the form y = mx + c and getting the gradient and y-intercept the wrong way round.
11148.correction: Graphing software can be used to show that adding a constant is a translation of the graph. Remind pupils that the y-intercept is when x is zero which is why it is the constant in the equation. They can substitute x = 0 to check.

4217.belief: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient.
4217.statement: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient.
4217.correction: Lines are parallel if they have the same gradient and different y-intercepts. Two lines are parallel if they are straight lines that are always the same non-zero distance apart.

2398.belief: Direct proportion can be determined by calculating the gradient.
2398.statement: Direct proportion can be determined by calculating the gradient.
2398.correction: The equation of the line should be of the form y = kx and so the y-intercept should be calculated to check it is zero.

9415.belief: Solutions for context-based problem can be listed as coordinate pairs with units e.g. 6 workers, 60 hours.
9415.statement: Solutions for context-based problem can be listed as coordinate pairs with units e.g. 6 workers, 60 hours.
9415.correction: Solutions should always be fully interpreted in relation to the context e.g. It would take 6 workers 60 hours to paint the building.

5964.statement: Pupils may not appreciate all the steps required to prove what type of shape is shown.
5964.correction: A warm-up for the lesson could be to review properties of shapes. Consider describing a shape, one property at a time. How much information is needed before pupils can be certain they know which shape is being described?

2488.belief: To draw a graph, points should always be joined with line segments.
2488.statement: To draw a graph, points should always be joined with line segments.
2488.correction: For the graph of $$y=x^3$$ show the line joining $$(0,0)$$ and $$(1,1)$$ and ask pupils to test some coordinate pairs from that line in the original equation. For example, $$(1/2,1/2)$$ does not satisfy the equation.

5316.correction: Encourage use of language such as "The turning point of this parabola is a maximum/minimum value" and "As the absolute values of $$x$$ increase, the $$y$$ values decrease/increase".

2.correction: Get pupils to consider what happens when $$x=1/2$$, $$x=1/3$$, $$x=1/4$$ etc. This will help them spot the role of the $$y$$ axis as asymptote for themselves.

3372.belief: A graph drawn on axes with no scale shown means nothing is known about the graph.
3372.statement: A graph drawn on axes with no scale shown means nothing is known about the graph.
3372.correction: Understanding the shape of a parabola, cubic curve, and reciprocal graph and then applying key features like positive/negative coefficients and $$y$$-intercepts enables pupils to infer much about the equation without needing actual coordinate values.

47.belief: 800 cm is further than 80 m because 800 is a larger number than 80.
47.statement: 800 cm is further than 80 m because 800 is a larger number than 80.
47.correction: Each unit of distance (e.g. cm, metre, km) describes a different-sized distance. 1 cm is 1/100 the size of a metre, meaning that 800 cm = 8 m is a shorter distance than 80 m.

5998.belief: Every scale increases by 1 each time or that there are 10 increments.
5998.statement: Pupils may assume every scale increases by 1 each time or that there are 10 increments.
5998.correction: Ensure pupils are counting how many gaps along the scale and calculating the increment size.

3000.belief: "To find the perimeter, you just add together the numbers that you see.".
3000.statement: "To find the perimeter, you just add together the numbers that you see."
3000.correction: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of all the sides of that shape. Not all sides have their lengths explicitly written. This could be due to sides having equal length, and the lengths of some sides shown with hash marks.

6957.statement: Pupils may miss an edge when calculating the perimeter.
6957.correction: Encourage the pupils to trace the perimeter to check that all edges have been included in the sum.

6468.statement: Pupils might find the area of parallelograms and triangles by multiplying the length of two adjacent edges which are not perpendicular.
6468.correction: Calculating the area of a shape involves multiplying two perpendicular lengths. These may not be horizontal and vertical in the shape's initial orientation.

7012.statement: Pupils may multiply all given lengths.
7012.correction: Remind pupils that area is found by multiplying two perpendicular lengths from the shape and in some cases a coefficient (half for a triangle, pi for a circle). Trapeziums use the mean length of the parallel sides (one length).

7481.statement: Pupils may struggle to select the correct process of perimeter or area.
7481.correction: Pupils should consider whether a space is to be covered in which case it is most likely area.

4202.belief: "Any line segment starting from the centre of a circle is a radius.".
4202.statement: "Any line segment starting from the centre of a circle is a radius."
4202.correction: It is true that one endpoint of a radius must be at the centre of a circle. However, the other endpoint must be on the circumference of the circle. This second endpoint cannot be inside or outside of the circle.

3008.belief: "When finding the perimeter of a sector, I need to multiply the radius by a fraction of a full circle, just like I did with the circumference to find the arc length.".
3008.statement: "When finding the perimeter of a sector, I need to multiply the radius by a fraction of a full circle, just like I did with the circumference to find the arc length."
3008.correction: Reminder that only part (the arc length) of the formula for perimeter of a sector varies with the angle. A desmos or geogebra model can help to show this.

2482.belief: If I double the radius of a sector, its area also doubles.
2482.statement: If I double the radius of a sector, its area also doubles.
2482.correction: The radius and area of a sector (or circle) do not share a linear relationship, so you cannot apply direct proportional reasoning. However, angle of a sector and its area do share a linear relationship, as long as the angle is ≤ 360°.

2526.belief: Due to the many thought processes involved with these questions, pupils may end up choosing the incorrect value as the radius for a sector.
2526.statement: Due to the many thought processes involved with these questions, pupils may end up choosing the incorrect value as the radius for a sector.
2526.correction: Encourage the use of words in their working e.g. "Diameter of shape A = 4 cm" or "Width of parallelogram = 6 mm" so when the numbers are needed again it is clear what each one is. If needed remind pupils of key word definitions such as radius.

3007.belief: When finding the perimeter of a rectilinear compound shape, pupils might sum the perimeters of each rectangle.
3007.statement: When finding the perimeter of a rectilinear compound shape, pupils might sum the perimeters of each rectangle.
3007.correction: Part of the perimeter for each rectangle is inside the compound shape. Therefore, not all of the perimeter of each rectangle contributes towards the perimeter of the compound shape in this problem.

7105.statement: Pupils read from the incorrect values on the protractor.
7105.correction: Encourage pupils to consider the type of angle they are measuring. If it is an acute angle, will it really measure 122°?

225.belief: Alternate angles are always equal to each other.
225.statement: Alternate angles are always equal to each other.
225.correction: Alternate angles are equal when a transversal intersects parallel lines. If the transversal intersects a pair of lines that are not parallel then the alternate angles will not be equal.

276.belief: Angles facts cannot be used with shapes as shapes have line segments rather than lines.
276.statement: Angles facts cannot be used with shapes as shapes have line segments rather than lines.
276.correction: It is the properties of the lines, such as whether they are parallel, that are important, not their length.

4805.belief: The name for a shape only applies to the regular version of that shape. E.g. An irregular pentagon is just a shape, as pentagons must have 5 equal sides.
4805.statement: The name for a shape only applies to the regular version of that shape. E.g. An irregular pentagon is just a shape, as pentagons must have 5 equal sides.
4805.correction: The name of a shape is known based on the number of sides and these do not have to be regular.

9354.belief: The size of an interior angle in a regular shape cannot be found unless the size of the other angles are given.
9354.statement: The size of an interior angle in a regular shape cannot be found unless the size of the other angles are given.
9354.correction: A regular shape has the property that all of its interior angles are equal in size. This means that the size of each interior angle is very easy to find if, for example, the sum of the interior angles is known.

2876.belief: An exterior angle is equal to 360° - the size of the interior angle because angles around a point sum to 360°.
2876.statement: An exterior angle is equal to 360° - the size of the interior angle because angles around a point sum to 360°.
2876.correction: An exterior angle is an angle on the outside of a polygon between an extension of an edge and the adjacent edge.

4213.belief: Lines cannot be added to the given diagram.
4213.statement: Lines cannot be added to the given diagram.
4213.correction: Often adding additional or found information to a given diagram can help progress towards a solution. Pupils should not be afraid to extend given line segments nor add notation if appropriate.

1965.belief: Congruent shapes are not similar shapes.
1965.statement: Congruent shapes are not similar shapes.
1965.correction: Congruent shapes are similar shapes. The scale factor, or multiplier, between them is one.

7190.statement: Pupils may rotate in the opposite direction to the stated direction.
7190.correction: Encourage pupils to read the question twice and highlight the key pieces of information before starting the question.

8665.statement: Pupils may write or read the column vector incorrectly by thinking the top element is for the vertical movement and the bottom element is for the horizontal movement.
8665.correction: Remind pupils that coordinates are horizontal before vertical and that is the same on a column vector.

6648.statement: Pupils may find reflecting across a diagonal line more challenging than vertically or horizontally.
6648.correction: Pupils may find it easier with tracing paper, or rotating their book/paper so the line of reflection is vertical.

6939.statement: Pupils may measure/count from the object rather than the centre of enlargement.
6939.correction: Have pupils check their answers using ray lines.

6938.statement: Pupils may measure/count from the object instead of the centre of enlargement.
6938.correction: Encourage pupils to check their answers by using ray lines.

5020.belief: The number of spaces to translate a shape can be worked out by counting the squares on the grid.
5020.statement: The number of spaces to translate a shape can be worked out by counting the squares on the grid.
5020.correction: If there are axes, then it is important to check the scales. The length of one square does not always represent one unit.

5179.belief: There is only one way to describe what has happened to an object to create its image.
5179.statement: There is only one way to describe what has happened to an object to create its image.
5179.correction: There may be multiple transformations or combinations of transformations that map the object to the image.

9630.belief: All straight line graphs show direct proportion.
9630.statement: All straight line graphs show direct proportion.
9630.correction: Only straight line graphs that pass through the origin (0, 0) show direct proportion.

3288.belief: "I will get different linear scale factors if a measure corresponding lengths in cm vs inches.".
3288.statement: "I will get different linear scale factors if a measure corresponding lengths in cm vs inches."
3288.correction: Scale factors do not have dimensions, and aren't linked to specific units. If one length is 23 cm (9 inches), and a corresponding length is 69 cm (27 inches), then the scale factor between them is 3, regardless of whether we measured in cm or inches.

6090.belief: Knowing the three angles is sufficient to prove two triangles are congruent.
6090.statement: Pupils may believe that knowing the three angles is sufficient to prove two triangles are congruent.
6090.correction: Use an equilateral triangle to show that, although two equilateral triangles have the same angles, they are not guaranteed to be congruent. In fact they are similar.

8453.statement: Pupils may try and use this criteria without knowing the angle between the two sides.
8453.correction: Pupils can construct triangles with two sides and an angle to see that there are two potential triangles, and therefore congruency is not guaranteed with SSA.

6918.statement: Pupils may make incorrect assumptions about diagrams containing a right angle.
6918.correction: Remind pupils that they cannot assume there is a right angle, just because two line segments look as if they are perpendicular to each other.

8760.belief: A ratio of 1: 400 for a scale model of a car to a real car will have units of cm and metres, because a scale model is measured in cm and a real car is measured in metres.
8760.statement: A ratio of 1: 400 for a scale model of a car to a real car will have units of cm and metres, because a scale model is measured in cm and a real car is measured in metres.
8760.correction: Unless the scale explicitly includes different units of measure for each part, you must always use the same unit for each part of a ratio. So, 1: 400 should be seen as 1 cm: 400 cm, not 400 metres, which is far too long for a car!

6341.statement: Pupils count all the triangles in a row to determine length rather than only counting the ones which have an edge on the line.
6341.correction: Encourage pupils to consider what they are using to measure when they draw each line on isometric paper.

5528.belief: The plan and elevations should look exactly the same on squared paper as they do on a solid drawn on isometric paper.
5528.statement: The plan and elevations should look exactly the same on squared paper as they do on a solid drawn on isometric paper.
5528.correction: The grid lines on the two types of paper are not the same which is why there is a visual difference. The measurements for each line however have not changed.

5529.belief: The plan and elevations show every aspect of a solid.
5529.statement: The plan and elevations show every aspect of a solid.
5529.correction: The plan and elevations do not show the features inside a solid.

2145.belief: Curves cannot be drawn on isometric paper.
2145.statement: Curves cannot be drawn on isometric paper.
2145.correction: It is perfectly possible to draw a curve on isometric paper.

4641.correction: The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right-angled triangle. It is always opposite the right-angle.

3717.correction: It can be helpful to scaffold the steps for any pupils who are struggling with rearranging.

7769.belief: Direction matters when determining the distance between two points.
7769.statement: Pupils may think that direction matters when determining the distance between two points.
7769.correction: Direction matters when dealing with displacement, not distance.

3718.correction: A ratio table can be helpful to see the relationship between the sides and therefore how to rearrange.

6250.statement: Pupils may confuse the opposite and adjacent sides.
6250.correction: The orientation of the right-angled triangle is not important. Identifying the known angle is what determines which is is the opposite and which is the adjacent.

10437.correction: Try evaluating sin(0) on your calculator. What answer do you get?

10760.correction: Encourage pupils to draw the right-angled triangle for the scenario if they are unsure so that they can label the sides and be confident about which trigonometric function is needed.

6208.statement: Pupils may not be confident in knowing whether to apply Pythagoras' theorem or a trigonometric ratio.
6208.correction: Encourage pupils to label the diagram with all the information they have and then consider what they can deduce.

4642.belief: Misinterpreting a scale, particularly if given with no units.
4642.statement: Misinterpreting a scale, particularly if given with no units.
4642.correction: Encourage pupils to carefully convert the scale into a more useful scale. E.g. writing 1: 20 0000 as 1 cm = 2 km

4921.belief: Neglecting to follow the 3 conventions of bearings. Particularly, going anticlockwise when given a bearing over 180 degrees.
4921.statement: Neglecting to follow the 3 conventions of bearings. Particularly, going anticlockwise when given a bearing over 180 degrees.
4921.correction: Pupils can be asked to stand and turn 90 degrees. Some will turn clockwise and some anticlockwise. This will create a discussion point about the direction being important. Having the clockwise convention means a direction does not need to be given.

6937.statement: Pupils do not measure the angle from North and simply measure the angle between two line segments.
6937.correction: Reiterate bearings are always measured from North, in a clockwise direction and stated as 3 figures. Encourage pupils to draw North on the correct position before attempting the question.

3034.belief: The first two binomials have to be multiplied first.
3034.statement: The first two binomials have to be multiplied first.
3034.correction: Look for features of the binomials that suggest which binomials will be easiest to multiply first. Any order will give the same final product but a particular order may reduce complexity.

610.belief: The constants in the binomials must sum to the coefficient of x and multiply to the constant in the quadratic.
610.statement: Believing the constants in the binomials must sum to the coefficient of x and multiply to the constant in the quadratic.
610.correction: Use an area model to show what is happening when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1. Pupils should always check their answers by expanding.

8434.statement: Pupils may try to factorise and solve without rearranging first.
8434.correction: Being able to put the factors equal to zero only makes sense if we are using the property that if two values multiply to zero, one of them is zero.

10021.belief: We subtract the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is positive and add the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is negative.
10021.statement: That we subtract the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is positive and add the constant squared when the constant in the bracket is negative.
10021.correction: Squaring a negative value gives a positive value. Whether the constant in the bracket is positive or negative, the square of the constant must always be subtracted. This can be made clearer with algebra tiles or area models.

6173.belief: To write in completed square form they can divide through by the coefficient of x^2.
6173.statement: Pupils may believe that to write in completed square form they can divide through by the coefficient of x^2
6173.correction: This works for equations as equality can be maintained by dividing both sides of the equation. However if manipulating an expression, dividing through by a value changes the expression. Instead a value can be 'factored out' as necessary.

4663.belief: Mistakes often occur when substituting into the quadratic formula with calculators, as pupils miss out brackets and change the priority of operations.
4663.statement: Mistakes often occur when substituting into the quadratic formula with calculators, as pupils miss out brackets and change the priority of operations.
4663.correction: Values should always be put in brackets when substituted. This avoids mistakes when squaring and subtracting negative values. It also makes it easier to change the values of a, b, and c when working on a new question.

6656.statement: Pupils find the two $$x$$ values after solving the combined quadratic and declare that the solution.
6656.correction: It is important to substitute both $$x$$ values back in to one of the original equations to find the corresponding $$y$$ values. Without these, the solutions are incomplete.

5305.belief: For a pair of simultaneous equations (one linear and one quadratic), there will always be two intersections and therefore two solutions.
5305.statement: For a pair of simultaneous equations (one linear and one quadratic), there will always be two intersections and therefore two solutions.
5305.correction: The linear graph might be tangent to the curve therefore only one intersection (solution). Alternatively, the straight line may never intersect the parabola and in this case, there is no solution.

466.belief: Assuming that the decimal part of the number will entirely disappear in the subtraction step.
466.statement: Assuming that the decimal part of the number will entirely disappear in the subtraction step.
466.correction: Ensure that pupils line up the decimal points and use squares in their books for each digit. This should allow pupils to see the parts that cancel each other out and what is left when finding the difference.

7009.statement: Pupils multiply the base by the fractional exponent. e.g 25^(1/2) = 12.5
7009.correction: The use of a calculator allows pupils to see the index of a fraction is not to be multiplied by the base. Embedding the laws of indices where two bases are the same and each number has an index of 1/2 helps recognize the 1/2 index as a square root.

6723.statement: Pupils may not fully simplify due to not identifying the highest square factor.
6723.correction: Encourage pupils to check the resulting radicand for any further square factors.

7011.statement: Pupils may not multiply the existing coefficient with the coefficient of the simplified surd.
7011.correction: Replace the unsimplified surd with the simplified form within the original expression so pupils can see they need to multiply coefficients.

7973.belief: Like surds need both the radicand and the coefficient to be the same.
7973.statement: Pupils may think like surds need both the radicand and the coefficient to be the same.
7973.correction: Remind them of the distributive law: a(b+c) = ab + ac.

7254.statement: Pupils may not simplify after multiplying surds.
7254.correction: Surds should always be written in their simplest form for the final answer.

6831.statement: Pupils may insist that a square root can be both positive and negative.
6831.correction: By convention, square root refers to the principal (positive) square root.

7308.statement: Pupils may struggle with applying the distributive law to expressions involving surds.
7308.correction: The area model can be used here to demonstrate how terms are multiplied when expanding the bracket.

7552.statement: Pupils may suggest using FOIL (or similar) to expand both brackets and make errors whilst doing so.
7552.correction: The grid method is derived from the area model and therefore the area model supports expanding both one binomial and two binomials.

8247.belief: The simplest form means a simplified surd as a denominator.
8247.statement: Pupils may think the simplest form means a simplified surd as a denominator.
8247.correction: A fraction is not fully simplified if the denominator contains a surd term and must be rationalised as is convention.

7480.statement: Pupils may struggle to see why using the difference of two squares is important.
7480.correction: The grid method for multiplication can be used to explore why two of the terms cancel each other.

8645.statement: Pupils may want to write rounded solutions when solving a quadratic equation.
8645.correction: Remind them of the importance of accuracy and further calculations.

8472.statement: Pupils may be uncertain how to solve problems with surds.
8472.correction: Many problems can be solved through reasoning what you know, such as fully simplifying a surd.

9634.belief: Stratified sampling is biased and therefore produces a bad sample.
9634.statement: Stratified sampling is biased and therefore produces a bad sample.
9634.correction: Stratified sampling is used to take a representative sample from the population. Selecting from within the strata can be done using a simple random sample.

7450.statement: Pupils may struggle to rearrange the equivalent fractions.
7450.correction: A ratio table may be easier for pupils to use instead.

9351.belief: For all situations the weightings are subjective.
9351.statement: That for all situations the weightings are subjective.
9351.correction: There are situations in which a subjective decision is made about weightings but there are also situations where the multipliers used are dictated by the context in a logical way. An example of this is combining groups and combining their means.

467.belief: Assuming that when dividing the UB will be the result of the UB ÷ UB.
467.statement: Assuming that when dividing the UB will be the result of the UB ÷ UB.
467.correction: Get the pupils to investigate dividing numbers. Keep the divisor the same and change the dividend. Ask the question, "What happens as the dividend increases?".

10447.belief: Truncating the numbers rather than rounding when considering the suitable degree of accuracy.
10447.statement: Truncating the numbers rather than rounding when considering the suitable degree of accuracy.
10447.correction: Emphasise that the numbers are being rounded and therefore the digit in the next decimal place must be considered.

11175.belief: When $$x: y$$ are in the ratio 1: 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$.
11175.statement: When $$x: y$$ are in the ratio 1: 2 pupils write the equation as $$x = 2y$$
11175.correction: The bar models shown in this lesson can help to support pupils with this.

5470.belief: Perpendicular lines have to be drawn as a horizontal and vertical pair.
5470.statement: Perpendicular lines have to be drawn as a horizontal and vertical pair.
5470.correction: Some pupils may struggle to see that two lines are perpendicular when they are not drawn horizontally and vertically. Drawing this on paper and then rotating the paper will help them see that it is the angle between the lines that matters.

3367.belief: The gradients of two perpendicular lines are a number and its reciprocal.
3367.statement: The gradients of two perpendicular lines are a number and its reciprocal.
3367.correction: In order for two lines to be perpendicular, the two gradients cannot have the same sign. Therefore it is a number and its negative reciprocal.

5291.belief: P is a point such that AP: PB is in the ratio of 1: 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
5291.statement: P is a point such that AP: PB is in the ratio of 1: 3 means that point P is a third of the distance of AB from A.
5291.correction: There are 4 equal parts in total, meaning that point P is a quarter of the distance of AB from A.

11179.belief: $$y=x^3$$ has one root so all cubic graphs have one root.
11179.statement: $$y=x^3$$ has one root so all cubic graphs have one root.
11179.correction: Make sure pupils see a wide variety of cubic graphs; ones with one root, two roots and three roots and link every one back to its equation and that the highest exponent of the variable is $$3$$ so they are all cubic graphs.

8794.belief: All reciprocal graphs appear only in two quadrants and have both axes as asymptotes.
8794.statement: All reciprocal graphs appear only in two quadrants and have both axes as asymptotes.
8794.correction: Show pupils the graphs of the $$y={1\over{x}}$$, then $$y={1\over{x}}+1$$, then $$y={1\over{x+1}}$$ and get them to compare which forms have which axes as asymptotes.

11176.correction: Remind pupils of the laws of indices that can be used to show that $$b^{0} = 1$$

11177.belief: $$y=b^x$$ will reach zero; the curve will touch the $$x$$ axis eventually.
11177.statement: $$y=b^x$$ will reach zero; the curve will touch the $$x$$ axis eventually.
11177.correction: Get pupils to input large absolute $$x$$ values to appreciate that no matter how small the $$y$$ value it is still a fraction greater than zero.

10779.belief: There is only value for $$y$$ for any given value of $$x$$.
10779.statement: There is only value for $$y$$ for any given value of $$x$$
10779.correction: Pythagoras' theorem on a coordinate grid shows that there are two possible places where the $$y$$-coordinate could be for any given value of $x$$. This is also true for the $$x$$-coordinate for any given value of $$y$$

10703.belief: Using the incorrect value for finding the percentage, for instance, the area of the unshaded when it asks for the shaded region.
10703.statement: Using the incorrect value for finding the percentage, for instance, the area of the unshaded when it asks for the shaded region.
10703.correction: Encourage pupils to underline/highlight whether they are finding the percentage of the shaded or unshaded region.

6410.statement: Some pupils may have an equivalent algebraic expressions without noticing.
6410.correction: Tell pupils to always check if their expressions can be simplified or factorised before deeming themselves incorrect.

3383.belief: "The graphs of two straight line equations should always intersect at integer points on a coordinate grid.".
3383.statement: "The graphs of two straight line equations should always intersect at integer points on a coordinate grid."
3383.correction: The location with which the graphs of two straight line equations intersect can be found by simultaneously solving the pair of equations. The graphs of two straight line equations can intersect at either integer or non-integer values.

5826.belief: For the problems with squares inscribed inside circles, pupils may think that the length of the square is equal to the diameter of the circle.
5826.statement: For the problems with squares inscribed inside circles, pupils may think that the length of the square is equal to the diameter of the circle.
5826.correction: This would be the case if the circle was inscribed inside a square. But when the square is inscribed inside a circle, the diagonal length of the square is equal to the diameter of the circle.

8052.belief: A negative scale factor creates a smaller image than the object.
8052.statement: Pupils may think that a negative scale factor creates a smaller image than the object.
8052.correction: Remind them that the absolute value will be less than 1 and greater than 0 to create a smaller image. Whether the scale factor is positive or negative does not affect this.

8647.statement: Pupils may want to write the transformation as two transformations, a rotation of 180° followed by an enlargement by a positive scale factor, rather than a single transformation.
8647.correction: Remind pupils that a single transformation is more efficient than multiple transformations.

4100.belief: If the length of an image is 4 times as long as its object, then its area will also be 4 times as big.
4100.statement: If the length of an image is 4 times as long as its object, then its area will also be 4 times as big.
4100.correction: If the scale factor between lengths is 4, then the area of the image will be 16 times as big. The scale factor between the length of an object and image is different to the multiplier that shows how the area of an object changes after enlargement.

4208.belief: A linear scale factor can only be found by finding the multiplicative relationship between two corresponding lengths.
4208.statement: A linear scale factor can only be found by finding the multiplicative relationship between two corresponding lengths.
4208.correction: A linear scale factor can also be found by square rooting an area scale factor, where an area scale factor is found from the multiplicative relationship between the area of two similar 2D shapes, or corresponding faces on two similar 3D shapes.

5156.belief: "One shape has an area that is 21% larger than another shape. I can't find the area scale factor between the shapes, since I don't know the actual area of either shape.".
5156.statement: "One shape has an area that is 21% larger than another shape. I can't find the area scale factor between the shapes, since I don't know the actual area of either shape."
5156.correction: It is possible to find scale factors, even if only a percentage that describes their areas is given. One shape will have an area of 100%, so the other shape will have an area 21% larger, at 121%. The scale factor is 1.21 because 100% × 1.21 = 121%.

7975.belief: Every line segment that touches a circle exactly once is a tangent (even when it is not perpendicular to the radius at that point).
7975.statement: Pupils may think that every line segment that touches a circle exactly once is a tangent (even when it is not perpendicular to the radius at that point).
7975.correction: If unsure, try extending the line segment to beyond the edges of the circle to check whether it would intersect the circle again.

2893.belief: When faced with a quadrilateral which has three vertices on a circle and one vertex at the centre, pupils may think that the interior angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
2893.statement: When faced with a quadrilateral which has three vertices on a circle and one vertex at the centre, pupils may think that the interior angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
2893.correction: The two angles need to be subtended by the same arc for this circle theorem to apply. Therefore, it is the reflex angle at the centre of the circle which is twice the angle at the circumference.

6728.statement: Pupils may over-generalise the circle theorem by assume that all triangles that are inscribed in a circle are right-angled.
6728.correction: The triangle is only right-angled if one of its angles is subtended by the diameter. This also means that if the triangle is right-angled, then its hypotenuse is the diameter of the circle.

5996.belief: A radius which intersects a chord always bisects the chord.
5996.statement: Pupils may assume that a radius which intersects a chord always bisects the chord.
5996.correction: A radius only bisects a chord if they are perpendicular.

6001.belief: Tangents can be drawn in slightly different directions at the same point on a circle.
6001.statement: Pupils may assume that tangents can be drawn in slightly different directions at the same point on a circle.
6001.correction: The tangent at a point on a circle can only be drawn in one possible direction. The tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at that point.

7123.statement: Pupils may reason that two angles are the same size, as they are subtended by the same chord.
7123.correction: Angles are equal, if they are in the same segment, subtended by the same arc, as well as subtended by the same chord.

6210.statement: Pupils may conflate the alternate segment theorem with alternate angles on parallel lines, thinking that the chord that meets the tangent is a transversal between two equal angles.
6210.correction: Alternate angles are only equal when the transversal is between parallel lines. In many of the examples for the alternate segment theorem, the tangent is not parallel to a chord.

6211.statement: Pupils may conflate cyclic quadrilaterals with cases of "the angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference" theorem, when the angle at the centre is a reflex angle.
6211.correction: While the two diagrams may look similar at a glance, pay extra attention to whether all four points of the quadrilateral are on the circumference or if one of the points is in the centre.

7702.belief: All circle theorems are about angles.
7702.statement: Pupils may think that all circle theorems are about angles.
7702.correction: Circle theorems can be about angles or lengths in diagrams containing a circle.

7131.statement: Pupils may not recognise or confuse which circle theorems to apply in a multi-step problem.
7131.correction: Encourage pupils to add more to a diagram in order to deduce more information about the problem. Drawing an additional line segment, such chord or radius may a useful first step.

8681.belief: Pythagoras' theorem cannot be applied to 3D shapes.
8681.statement: Pythagoras' theorem cannot be applied to 3D shapes.
8681.correction: Pupils may benefit from imaging the cuboid is 'sliced' through and a triangle drawn on the now visible face.

10436.belief: Trigonometric ratios cannot be applied to 3D shapes.
10436.statement: Trigonometric ratios cannot be applied to 3D shapes.
10436.correction: Pupils may benefit from imaging the cuboid is 'sliced' through and a triangle drawn on the now visible face.

9419.belief: When solving equations with fractional coefficients, pupils may divide by the reciprocal rather than multiply. E.g. $$\\frac{1}{2}x = 8$$ pupils may just halve $$8$$.
9419.statement: When solving equations with fractional coefficients, pupils may divide by the reciprocal rather than multiply. E.g. $$\\frac{1}{2}x = 8$$ pupils may just halve $$8$$
9419.correction: Start with integer coefficients, and get pupils used to the idea of multiplying by the reciprocal (not just dividing by the coefficient). This step should be written as part of the working. Answers can be checked by substitution.

6946.statement: Pupils may misconfigure the net, believing that as long as the shapes of the faces are correct, the net will fold to be the desired 3D shape.
6946.correction: Have pupils mark/label/colour the edges that will join upon folding the net, this will ensure they are the correct length.

8712.belief: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
8712.statement: When questions are in context, the length may be described as the depth or height and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
8712.correction: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. They may need to evaluate a perpendicular length from other given information, using trigonometry or Pythagoras' theorem.

11124.belief: When working out the surface area, the pupil may only find the sum of the areas of three faces of a cuboid (for example the visible sides in a 3D drawing), instead of all six faces.
11124.statement: When working out the surface area, the pupil may only find the sum of the areas of three faces of a cuboid (for example the visible sides in a 3D drawing), instead of all six faces.
11124.correction: Encourage pupils to sketch the net of the cuboid as part of their solution. This will provide a visual reminder to the pupil to find the area of all six faces, as well as making it easier to check their answer.

6958.statement: Pupils can miss out some faces of the prism when calculating the surface area.
6958.correction: Encourage pupils to sketch out the net of the prism and label it clearly, to ensure that they include all faces in their calculation of the surface area. This will allow their answer to be checked more easily.

8711.belief: When questions are in context, the height of the cylinder may be described as the depth or length and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
8711.statement: When questions are in context, the height of the cylinder may be described as the depth or length and this can cause some pupils to struggle if they have learned a formula with a particular word.
8711.correction: Remind pupils that the volume of a 3D shape comes from the area of a cross section multiplied by the height or depth. Discuss which length this would be, using a diagram to support.

6912.statement: Pupils can make errors if given the dimensions/measurements of the cylinder using different units (for example the radius is given in cm and the length in m).
6912.correction: Remind pupils to convert all measurements to the same unit (such as cm or m) before starting the calculation. Usually there is a prompt in the question to use as a guide, for example give your answer in square centimetres.

7728.statement: Pupils may think that a cone is a pyramid.
7728.correction: Remind pupils that a pyramid has a polygonal base, so a cone cannot be a pyramid as the base is a circle, which is not a polygon.

8555.statement: Pupils may use the edge length as the perpendicular height when calculating the volume.
8555.correction: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and in most pyramids the edge of a triangle is not perpendicular to the base. Also the edge of the triangles can be different in the pyramid.

6687.statement: Pupils may forget the constant '4' when calculating the surface area.
6687.correction: Show the demonstration of the formula of the surface area using a different spherical fruit to see that it is always 4 regardless of the size of the sphere. You can also relate it to the 1/2 in the formula of the area of triangle.

7017.statement: Pupils may multiply the radius of the sphere by the constant before cubing it.
7017.correction: Remind pupils of the order of operations and the need to cube the radius before multiplying by the constants in the formula.

3014.belief: When finding the surface area of the cone, pupils may find the curved surface area but forget to include circular base of the cone.
3014.statement: When finding the surface area of the cone, pupils may find the curved surface area but forget to include circular base of the cone.
3014.correction: By re-reading the question, and inspecting any given diagram, pupils can check if the cone is open or closed and therefore if they need to include the circular base in their calculation.

6268.statement: Pupils may confuse the slant height (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone) with the perpendicular height (which is needed to find the volume of the cone).
6268.correction: Remind pupils that for any volume calculation, three perpendicular lengths are multiplied and the slant height is not perpendicular to the base in a right cone. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem to find the perpendicular height.

7547.statement: Pupils may not subtract overlapping faces from their surface area calculation.
7547.correction: Ask the pupils to visualise turning around/rotating the compound solid, and consider which faces of the component solids would always be hidden.

8615.statement: Pupils may only using given measures in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required for substitution into a volume formula.
8615.correction: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to show how the are breaking down a compound/composite shape. Pupils should label the diagram with any new lengths needed. They may need to use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find these new lengths.

6284.statement: Pupils may confuse whether they need to calculate the volume or surface area of a 3D shape, if not told specifically to do so in a problem.
6284.correction: Use the context to decide which calculation is needed. If the question refers to packaging or painting the shape, a surface area calculation is needed.

7047.statement: Pupils may omit outcomes or include repetitions of the same outcomes in their lists.
7047.correction: For each problem, encourage pupils to be systematic with their ordering of outcomes.

8241.belief: Any set of probabilities relating to a scenario will always sum to 1.
8241.statement: Pupils may think that any set of probabilities relating to a scenario will always sum to 1.
8241.correction: Probabilities sum to 1 when the events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

8540.statement: Pupils may be unsure whether a variable represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcome.
8540.correction: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what any variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).

7573.statement: Pupils may be tempted to always use the total frequency from a tree as the denominator of any fraction.
7573.correction: The denominator of the fraction should be the total frequency of the group that is being selected from. This could be the total population or it could be a subgroup of the population.

6746.statement: Pupils may get confused between two-way tables that show outcomes and two-way tables that show frequencies (particularly when the outcomes are numbers, such as the sum of two dice rolls).
6746.correction: Two-way tables can be either used to display the sample space of individual outcomes or the frequencies of outcomes. Therefore, when using a table, it can be helpful to note down what type of data the table shows.

5947.statement: Pupils may add the probabilities along branches of a probability tree, rather than multiplying them.
5947.correction: Remind pupils that probabilities cannot be greater than 1 and demonstrate that adding across the branches sometimes results in a probability that is greater than 1. Therefore, it must be wrong.

5278.belief: If outcome A occurs more often than outcome B, during an experiment, pupils may conclude that outcome A has a greater probability of occurring than outcome B in future trials.
5278.statement: If outcome A occurs more often than outcome B, during an experiment, pupils may conclude that outcome A has a greater probability of occurring than outcome B in future trials.
5278.correction: Even when two outcomes are equally likely to happen, one may occur more often than the other due to chance. You could be more confident about your conclusion if you observe a large difference in results in an experiment with a large number of trials.

5995.belief: It possible to determine whether a coin (or other object/game) is biased by conducting an experiment with a small number of trials.
5995.statement: Pupils may assume that it possible to determine whether a coin (or other object/game) is biased by conducting an experiment with a small number of trials.
5995.correction: The greater the number of trial that an experiment contains, the closer the relative frequency of an outcome gets to its theoretical probability.

7644.belief: A ∪ B means 'to be either from A or B (but not both)'.
7644.statement: Pupils may think that A ∪ B means 'to be either from A or B (but not both)'.
7644.correction: A ∪ B represents all members that satisfy at least one of the events A or B. So it could be from A, from B or from both A and B.

6212.statement: Pupils may conflate the meaning of mutually exclusive with the meaning of independent.
6212.correction: Emphasise the word 'exclusive' in 'mutually exclusive' to suggest that one event excludes the other. Also, emphasise that the opposite of independent is dependent.

6259.statement: Pupils may confuse the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), with the probability of event A and B occurring.
6259.correction: Use the context of the question to make a judgement about what probability is to be calculated. Try to avoid using, or draw attention to, potentially ambiguous language/notation. E.g. Is P(AB) referring to P(A given B) or P(B given A) or P(A and B)?

6319.belief: When pupils construct probability trees for scenarios where two marbles are removed from a bag, they may mistakenly subtract 2 from the denominators of the probabilities instead of 1.
6319.statement: When pupils construct probability trees for scenarios where two marbles are removed from a bag, they may mistakenly subtract 2 from the denominators of the probabilities instead of 1.
6319.correction: Even though two marbles are removed from the bag at once, you can think of it at choosing one marble and then immediately choosing a second marble. At the end of the process, two marbles have been removed.

7184.statement: Pupils may represent probabilities in the wrong position on the probability scale by miscounting the number of intervals required.
7184.correction: Before using any probability scale, it can be helpful to make a note of the sizes for each major and minor interval.

1991.belief: When considering meter readings, using the 'new reading' rather than the units used to calculate the cost.
1991.statement: When considering meter readings, using the 'new reading' rather than the units used to calculate the cost.
1991.correction: Emphasise that it is the change in readings that indicates the units used during a time period. The 'new reading' alone shows the total number of units used since the meter was installed.

2536.belief: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes.
2536.statement: E.g 4.5 hours is 4 hours and 50 minutes
2536.correction: Encouraging pupils to use ratio tables to represent proportional relationships using minutes allows them to appreciate the multiplier of 60 when converting hours to minutes, or minutes to seconds.

3308.belief: Giving a density answer in the wrong units.
3308.statement: Giving a density answer in the wrong units.
3308.correction: Read the question carefully and check the units of the mass and the volume. It may be necessary to convert between metric units.

10747.belief: Using the total surface area of the solid rather than the area of the solid that is in contact with the floor/table.
10747.statement: Using the total surface area of the solid rather than the area of the solid that is in contact with the floor/table.
10747.correction: Refer back to the high-heeled shoe and elephants foot example. This should clarify that it is the area in contact with the foot that increases or decreases the pressure.

513.belief: The average speed is found by adding the speeds and dividing by how many average speeds are given.
513.statement: The average speed is found by adding the speeds and dividing by how many average speeds are given.
513.correction: The common misconception is calculating an average of an average. Show how the answers when calculating the average of the average speeds is not the same as calculating the average speed using the total distance and total time of the average speeds.

8508.statement: Pupils understand they multiply by 100 when converting m to cm, but when converting m^2 to cm^2, fail to recognise the need to multiply by 100^2. This is also the same with volume conversions.
8508.correction: Illustrate a 1m^2 square and the equivalent 100cm^2 square, calculating the area and allowing pupils to see the equivalence of 1 m^2 = 10 000 cm^2. Also apply this to a 1m^3 and 100cm^3, thus allowing students to see 1m^2 = 100 000 cm^3.

4090.belief: Leaving out key information when sketching graphs.
4090.statement: Leaving out key information when sketching graphs.
4090.correction: Although sketches do not need to be to scale they do need to contain all key information. Getting pupils to write these on as coordinate pairs is the clearest way. Sketches still have to be useful for the purpose of a model.

4296.belief: Not looking at units when calculating the gradient of the line to find speed.
4296.statement: Not looking at units when calculating the gradient of the line to find speed.
4296.correction: A recap on compound measures and units may be helpful here. The units of compound measures tell us how to calculate the measure. E.g. km/h is the distance in km/ time in hours. Pupils need to check the units on their graphs and convert if needed.

7898.belief: A horizontal line on a speed-time means the object is stationary.
7898.statement: Pupils may think a horizontal line on a speed-time means the object is stationary.
7898.correction: The $$y$$ axis is plotting speed so a horizontal line means the speed has not changed in that time. But this can be at any speed. Pupils need to double check axes to know what sort of graph they are using.

3835.belief: Interpolation is always more accurate than extrapolation.
3835.statement: Interpolation is always more accurate than extrapolation.
3835.correction: If a graph is plotting data collected at set points then there is no way to know what is happening between the points. The trend between the points could be a curve, a line or could fluctuate. Interpolation could therefore be inaccurate.

4480.belief: When matching, or sketching, distance-time and speed-time graphs pupils may think these have a similar shape.
4480.statement: When matching, or sketching, distance-time and speed-time graphs pupils may think these have a similar shape.
4480.correction: Questioning helps. Ask pupils to explain what is happening on a variety of graphs. For example, "A diagonal line with positive gradient on a speed-time graph. What is happening?" "A horizontal line on distance-time graph. What is happening?"

471.belief: Assuming that any linear graph with a constant positive gradient shows a directly proportional relationship.
471.statement: Assuming that any linear graph with a constant positive gradient shows a directly proportional relationship.
471.correction: Using examples in a context really helps here. E.g. 'I change £0. How many dollars do I get?, I travel 0 miles. How many kilometres have I travelled?

469.belief: Assuming the the graph will eventually intercept the axes.
469.statement: Assuming the the graph will eventually intercept the axes.
469.correction: Pupils can experiment with very large numbers. Here a spreadsheet is useful to generate numbers very quickly and show that although it gets very close to zero it never actually gets there.

226.belief: Alternating sequences may cause difficulty if negative number skills are not secure.
226.statement: Alternating sequences may cause difficulty if negative number skills are not secure.
226.correction: A review of negative numbers would be useful. Prior lessons can be used for this review if required.

379.belief: Arithmetic sequences only have a positive integer as the common difference.
379.statement: Arithmetic sequences only have a positive integer as the common difference.
379.correction: Arithmetic sequences can be increasing or decreasing and can have any value for the common difference.

4262.belief: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
4262.statement: As long as the equation can be solved, the value will be in the sequence.
4262.correction: For the value to be in the sequence, the value for $$n$$ must be a positive integer. If it is not, then the value is not in the sequence as the term number must be a positive integer.

7192.statement: Pupils may round the wrong way when finding the term number for a particular term value.
7192.correction: By calculating the terms either side of the non-integer value of $$n$$, pupils can easily determine what the rounded value of $$n$$ should be.

5608.belief: When plotting a sequence you should always connect the points with a line.
5608.statement: When plotting a sequence you should always connect the points with a line.
5608.correction: Only the (term number, term value) should be plotted. Points should not be joined as these are discrete values.

1810.belief: The common multiplier must be a positive integer for the sequence to be geometric.
1810.statement: The common multiplier must be a positive integer for the sequence to be geometric.
1810.correction: The multiplier needs to be the same between consecutive terms but it can be any value. Examples of this can be seen in the lesson.

4755.belief: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%.
4755.statement: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 3%
4755.correction: A multiplier of 1.3 is used to increase a value by 30%

6997.statement: Pupils may mix-up the x and y coordinates.
6997.correction: Remind pupils that the x value is read from the x-axis and is read first. The y value is read from the y-axis and is read second.

3715.correction: A filled in circle means the value is valid. An empty circle means the inequality is strict.

2429.belief: Dividing or multiplying by -1 does not change the inequality sign.
2429.statement: Dividing or multiplying by -1 does not change the inequality sign.
2429.correction: 2 < 3 becomes -2 > -3 when both sides are multiplied by -1.

3714.belief: Incorrectly interpreting inequalities due to the phrasing in English.
3714.statement: Incorrectly interpreting inequalities due to the phrasing in English.
3714.correction: It can be helpful to think about the context when interpreting the phrasing. If a speed limit of 30 mph, would it be acceptable to do more than 30 mph? Is the car allowed to travel at a lower speed at any point?

3822.belief: We are only interested in points that are in the region satisfied by all inequalities.
3822.statement: We are only interested in points that are in the region satisfied by all inequalities.
3822.correction: With practical contexts, such as project management, it is useful to know when one constraint is not being met as it can suggest where additional resources (if available) should be allocated.

2261.belief: When describing the movement of vectors, "across" is used to describe a horizontal movement.
2261.statement: When describing the movement of vectors, "across" is used to describe a horizontal movement.
2261.correction: Embed the understanding that "across" refers to the horizontal component, but the direction must be described concisely as a vector has direction and magnitude.

5318.belief: Parallel vectors can only be in the same direction.
5318.statement: Parallel vectors can only be in the same direction.
5318.correction: Two vectors are parallel if one can be written as a scalar multiple of the other. This scalar multiple can be negative therefore the direction can be opposite, but the gradients remain equivalent.

805.belief: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors,.
805.statement: When calculating the resultant vector, pupils can incorrectly sum vectors due to opposite directions or proportions of vectors,
805.correction: Encourage pupils to write a clear vector pathway: using highlighters can help to visualise this pathway.

8827.belief: A reflection of a vector in the x or y axis is not the reverse of a vector. This is often seen with equilateral triangles and vectors.
8827.statement: A reflection of a vector in the x or y axis is not the reverse of a vector. This is often seen with equilateral triangles and vectors.
8827.correction: When multiplying the vectors by -1 this gives the opposite direction of the vector only. The magnitude remains the same. Investigate with pupils by drawing column vectors and multiply by -1 and compare.

10722.belief: When using operations with vectors, pupils do not use the priority of operations.
10722.statement: When using operations with vectors, pupils do not use the priority of operations.
10722.correction: The priority of operations applies to all calculations.

4796.belief: "My construction didn't accurately bisect the line segment".
4796.statement: "My construction didn't accurately bisect the line segment"
4796.correction: Check that your compasses construct a full circle, and do not slip (and create a spiral-shape). Tighten the screw on your compasses, if possible. Then, if only using construction arcs that look confusing, you can construct full circles to help.

8576.statement: Pupils may use a protractor rather than a pair of compasses.
8576.correction: Remind pupils that a construction is done using a pair of compasses and ruler.

8432.statement: Pupils may try to draw the triangle using only a pencil and ruler, rather than construct it using a pair of compasses.
8432.correction: Remind pupils that if the task is to 'construct' then they must use their geometry equipment.

7132.statement: Some pupils may not recognise that they have constructed congruent triangles to one and another.
7132.correction: Use a piece of tracing paper to show that the triangles are congruent to each other.

8639.statement: Pupils may want to use a protractor to draw a right angle.
8639.correction: Remind pupils that they need to construct the right angle with a pair of compasses and a ruler, using appropriate construction techniques.

8574.statement: Pupils may not use a pair of compasses to find the two positions of the third vertex and instead just try to use their ruler.
8574.correction: You could encourage them to draw the circle before the angle each time.

7979.belief: The locus of a line is a rectangle.
7979.statement: Pupils may think that the locus of a line is a rectangle.
7979.correction: Choose the vertices of their rectangle and ask if they are the same distance from the line as another point. Link to Pythagoras' theorem if necessary to highlight that the diagonal length will be longer.

6107.belief: There is only one point which is equidistant from two points.
6107.statement: Pupils may believe that there is only one point which is equidistant from two points.
6107.correction: Highlight that forming any isosceles triangle will mean that that the point is equidistant from both points.

6411.statement: Pupils may erase their construction marks.
6411.correction: Remind pupils that they should always leave their construction marks on their diagrams but encourage them not to press to hard with their pencils.

6306.statement: Pupils may not consider that, in some contexts (e.g. a corded lawnmower), the shape of the locus will include sectors of different radii, if a shape/object is creating a barrier.
6306.correction: Have pupils consider the impact of going around the corner of a shape.

9297.belief: Simplifying $$\\frac{(x+4)}{(x+5)}$$ by crossing out the $$x$$ terms and getting $$\\frac{4}{5}$$.
9297.statement: Simplifying $$\\frac{(x+4)}{(x+5)}$$ by crossing out the $$x$$ terms and getting $$\\frac{4}{5}$$
9297.correction: Refrain from crossing out factors. Instead pupils should write the numerator and denominator as products of the hightest common factor and see that HCF/HCF = 1.

10454.belief: Trying to simplify a division calculation by identifying common factors before calculating.
10454.statement: Trying to simplify a division calculation by identifying common factors before calculating.
10454.correction: Pupils need to understand why this works with multiplication questions to understand why this does not work with division. Encourage pupils to write their division as a multiplication of the reciprocal before identifying common factors.

465.belief: Assuming that 'cross multiplying' is always the best way to solve equations with fractions on both sides.
465.statement: Assuming that 'cross multiplying' is always the best way to solve equations with fractions on both sides.
465.correction: Examples are included in the lesson where this results in unnecessary quadratic equations. Factorising and looking for common factors allows pupils to spot efficient methods. This also links with fraction skills of finding a common denominator.

8197.statement: Pupils may think that the reciprocal of $$\\frac{1}{a} + \\frac{1}{b}$$ is $$a + b$$
8197.correction: $$\\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{4} = \\frac{3}{4}$$ which is not the reciprocal of 2 + 4 = 6. To find the reciprocal, it helps for the expression to be written as a single fraction.

3189.belief: Not fully isolating the required variable by leaving other terms containing the variable in the expression.
3189.statement: Not fully isolating the required variable by leaving other terms containing the variable in the expression.
3189.correction: To make a variable the subject, it must be expressed in terms of other variables only. Factorising helps isolate a variable if it is in multiple terms.

10289.belief: The multiplier for a 2% increase is either 0.02 or 1.2.
10289.statement: Thinking the multiplier for a 2% increase is either 0.02 or 1.2
10289.correction: A 2% increase is 100% + 2% of the original amount. 102% is equivalent to 1.02 as a decimal.

8564.statement: Pupils may use the incorrect trigonometric formula.
8564.correction: Encourage pupils to label their triangles with the name for each side. This helps to identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.

7584.statement: Pupils may have their calculator set to radians instead of degrees.
7584.correction: The first check for understanding is designed to catch this but it is worth checking that the correct unit of measurement is being used throughout the lesson.

5983.belief: The graph displayed always shows the number of solutions.
5983.statement: Pupils assume that the graph displayed always shows the number of solutions.
5983.correction: It is important to compare the range of values that the graph is displaying against what is being defined in the question.

10749.belief: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
10749.statement: Using any two side lengths for the sine formula.
10749.correction: It must be two side lengths and the angle between them. So any two side lengths of the triangle can be used so long as you also use the angle between them.

8469.statement: Pupils may be uncertain about which angle pairs with which side.
8469.correction: The angle is paired with the side length that is opposite.

7230.statement: Pupils may not see the need for this rule as they have the sine rule.
7230.correction: The sine rule can be used in many cases but it is not always the most efficient. There will be problems where it will be much faster to use the cosine rule.

8473.statement: Pupils may be uncertain over how to start a problem.
8473.correction: Encourage pupils to draw a diagram if one is not provided and then to annotate the diagram with any given information as a first step. If a diagram is given then pupils should annotate that.

6770.statement: Pupils may be hesitant to start the problems due to uncertainty.
6770.correction: Encourage pupils to try an approach and then reflect on whether there has been progress towards a solution. Deducing something you didn't already know if progress even if it does not seem like it.

8343.belief: They have to use the sine or cosine rule.
8343.statement: Pupils may think that they have to use the sine or cosine rule.
8343.correction: Encourage pupils to consider all the trigonometric knowledge they have and choose the most appropriate piece for the problem they are dealing with.

7750.belief: If you cut the height of the cone in a half, the resulting frustrum will have half the volume of the original cone.
7750.statement: Pupils may think that if you cut the height of the cone in a half, the resulting frustrum will have half the volume of the original cone.
7750.correction: The frustrum is actually seven eighths of the volume of the original cone; the small cone that was removed to create the frustrum is one eighth the volume of the original cone if the frustrum and the small cone have the same height.

6269.statement: Pupils may confuse the slant length (which is needed to find the curved surface area of the cone or frustum) with the perpendicular (or vertical) height.
6269.correction: Encourage pupils to clearly label their diagrams, indicating the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol. They may need to use Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry to calculate the slant length.
