8614.statement: Pupils may only using given measures or terms in their calculations, even when these are not the lengths required to form an expression for the volume or surface area.
8614.correction: Encourage pupils to annotate diagrams to clearly show how the are breaking down a compound shape, and label clearly any new or missing lengths they can determine.

10787.belief: When variables are used in diagrams, pupils may be unsure whether it represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcomes.
10787.statement: When variables are used in diagrams, pupils may be unsure whether it represents a probability, frequency or a particular outcomes.
10787.correction: Variables can be used to represent either of these pieces of information. It can be helpful to start a problem by writing down what the variables represent (e.g. "Let x = the total number of marbles).

4310.belief: There is often a lot of information to process, in order to complete a three event Venn diagram accurately. Pupils may confuse which region to complete.
4310.statement: There is often a lot of information to process, in order to complete a three event Venn diagram accurately. Pupils may confuse which region to complete.
4310.correction: A three event Venn diagram is easier to complete if information from intersecting events is completed first.

6762.statement: Pupils may give the probability as a fraction with the wrong denominator.
6762.correction: Check that pupils understand the difference between the probability of event A given B, P(A|B), and the probability of event A and B occurring.

8083.belief: Only one type of diagram/table can be used to represent each probability problem and worry about choosing the correct one.
8083.statement: Pupils may think that only one type of diagram/table can be used to represent each probability problem and worry about choosing the correct one.
8083.correction: Emphasise that the same probability problem can often be represented using multiple diagrams or tables. In many cases, they will be able to find what they are looking for in any representation but it may be clearer to see in some more than others.

10730.belief: When using the product rule, pupils may be unsure whether they should divide the product by 2.
10730.statement: When using the product rule, pupils may be unsure whether they should divide the product by 2.
10730.correction: Pay extra attention to the context of the problem. If the order of the two outcomes is irrelevant, then you should divide by two. If each of the two outcomes is allocated to a separate event (e.g. 1st and 2nd) then do not divide by 2.

7878.belief: The gradient of the line to model simple interest is always the interest rate.
7878.statement: Pupils may think the gradient of the line to model simple interest is always the interest rate.
7878.correction: This works when investing £100 but not with other start values. The gradient is the amount of interest added each time which depends on the amount invested and the interest rate. There are examples to show this in the lesson.

3364.belief: Gradient is change in $$y$$ divided by change in $$x$$.
3364.statement: Gradient is change in $$y$$ divided by change in $$x$$.
3364.correction: The gradient is calculated by considering the change in $$y$$ when moving one unit in the positive $$x$$ direction.

6412.statement: Pupils may estimate negative gradients incorrectly by drawing gradient triangles the wrong way round or ignoring the fact that the $$y$$ values are decreasing as $$x$$ increases.
6412.correction: Pupils should look at the shape of the graph between two points and decide if it is positive or negative before calculating. If $$y$$ is decreasing as $$x$$ increases then the gradient is negative.

8310.belief: A tangent to a curve at a given point cannot intersect the curve at another point.
8310.statement: Pupils may think a tangent to a curve at a given point cannot intersect the curve at another point.
8310.correction: Define the tangent at a point as the line which has the same gradient as the curve at that point. If the graph is cubic then it is possible for the tangent at a point to intersect the graph again. There are examples in the lesson that show this.

7701.belief: A circle with equation $$(x+a)^2 + (y+b)^2=r^2$$ has centre $$(a,b)$$.
7701.statement: Pupils may think that a circle with equation $$(x+a)^2 + (y+b)^2=r^2$$ has centre $$(a,b)$$
7701.correction: The general form of an equation of a circle is $$(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2=r^2$$ where $$(a,b)$$ is then the centre. Graphing software will be useful to show and explore this general form.

6235.statement: Pupils can confuse the gradient of the radius with the length of the radius.
6235.correction: A sketch will help pupils apply the right skills. To find the equation of a straight line we need the gradient. You may wish to draw concentric circles to show pupils that the radii are different lengths but can have same gradient.

798.belief: Calculating area by counting squares rather than looking at the scales.
798.statement: Calculating area by counting squares rather than looking at the scales.
798.correction: Remind pupils that often on speed-time graphs the scales on the axes will be different. Check the scales before calculating distance. Check the final answer is realistic in context.

9739.belief: When students find an area they are used to communicating the answer in units$$^2$$. The area under a speed-time graph tells us the distance travelled though.
9739.statement: When students find an area they are used to communicating the answer in units$$^2$$. The area under a speed-time graph tells us the distance travelled though.
9739.correction: On the graph the base is time and the height is speed which is distance over time. Distance over time, multiplied by time, leaves just distance.

7224.belief: When pupils see four, five or six trapezia they want to work each one out individually, then, do another calculation adding those four, five, six areas together.
7224.statement: When pupils see four, five or six trapezia they want to work each one out individually, then, do another calculation adding those four, five, six areas together.
7224.correction: This is hugely inefficient. Write out the sum of the area of multiple trapeziums then, from there, look for efficiencies. This is where applying knowledge of factorisation can be beneficial as it reduces the work.

3841.belief: The intersection of two different graphs on a speed-time graph is the point where the faster particle overtakes the slower moving particle.
3841.statement: The intersection of two different graphs on a speed-time graph is the point where the faster particle overtakes the slower moving particle.
3841.correction: Remind pupils that this is a speed-time graph and ask, "How do we find the distance travelled on a speed-time graph?". Then, ask pupils to calculate how far each particle has travelled at the point of intersection.

10651.belief: We use the term 'multiplicative relationship' when talking about direct proportion. Pupils may need reminding that division is equivalent to multiplying by the reciprocal.
10651.statement: We use the term 'multiplicative relationship' when talking about direct proportion. Pupils may need reminding that division is equivalent to multiplying by the reciprocal.
10651.correction: Allow opportunities to explore division of a number and multiplication of its reciprocal. Remind pupils that any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1.

2905.belief: Failing to recognise that x/2 is the same as 1/2 × x and therefore shows a directly proportional relationship where the value of k is 1/2.
2905.statement: Failing to recognise that x/2 is the same as 1/2 × x and therefore shows a directly proportional relationship where the value of k is 1/2.
2905.correction: It is useful to go back to looking at unit fractions. E.g. 2/3 = 1/3 × 2 and 7/9 = 1/9 × 7, etc. And, then look at algebraic terms leading up to for example, 2x/3. 'What is the the multiplier?'

9222.belief: Setting up the initial proportion statement and hence the general form of the equation the wrong way around.
9222.statement: Setting up the initial proportion statement and hence the general form of the equation the wrong way around.
9222.correction: Pay particularly attention to the language used. Give pupils the opportunity to verbalise what different proportion statements mean. E.g. y ∝ x^2, 'read this aloud using the correct mathematical vocabulary'.

2392.belief: For all direct and inverse proportions, the multiplicative relationship is with x and y.
2392.statement: For all direct and inverse proportions, the multiplicative relationship is with x and y.
2392.correction: The multiplicative relationship whether direct or inverse can be shown as y and x^n. Show a ratio table of y and 1/x^2 and a table of y and 1/x. The inverse multiplicative relationship is seen with y and 1/x^2 and not with 1/x.

1995.belief: The constant of proportionality shows the gradient for inversely proportional graphs.
1995.statement: The constant of proportionality shows the gradient for inversely proportional graphs.
1995.correction: The constant of proportionality shows the gradient for directly proportional graphs only. The constant for a reciprocal graph in the form k/x^n, shows the distance of the reciprocal from the origin.

2406.belief: Directly proportional graphs all start from (0,0) and are above the y axis.
2406.statement: Directly proportional graphs all start from (0,0) and are above the y axis.
2406.correction: Directly proportional means there is a multiplier between y and x. This graph is always y=kx and is linear passing through (0,0). A proportionality graphs show the multiplicative relationship between y and x^n and can be linear and non linear.

6226.statement: Pupils may confuse the domain and the range.
6226.correction: Drawing the graph of the function and labelling the axes correctly will help pupils connect domain and range.

1931.belief: Confusing domain and range when considering the inverse function.
1931.statement: Confusing domain and range when considering the inverse function.
1931.correction: The range of a function is the domain of its inverse function.

8433.statement: Pupils may try to evaluate composite functions by working from left to right.
8433.correction: Remind pupils that they cannot do this as each function needs an input and with composite functions the input needs to be evaluated before it can be used.

9376.belief: Small slips in working can lead to the wrong answer and pupils are not clear on how to check their working.
9376.statement: Small slips in working can lead to the wrong answer and pupils are not clear on how to check their working.
9376.correction: The lesson models how to check working so that the correct answer can be verified. This is good practice and helps pupils identify if there is an error.

1934.belief: Confusing the order in which functions are evaluated.
1934.statement: Confusing the order in which functions are evaluated.
1934.correction: Pupils can substitute their answer into the composite function to check their answer. Putting brackets around the functions can help with confirming the order.

7596.belief: It is acceptable to use the same letter for all expressions.
7596.statement: Pupils may think it is acceptable to use the same letter for all expressions.
7596.correction: It may be acceptable for the letter to be the same but that depends on what the letter is representing.

1967.belief: Conjectures have to be correct so it's really hard to make a conjecture as you don't want to be wrong.
1967.statement: Conjectures have to be correct so it's really hard to make a conjecture as you don't want to be wrong.
1967.correction: Conjectures are thought to be true but they may not be. This is why we test and see ways to prove whether a conjecture is true or not. It is perfectly acceptable for a conjecture to be proved wrong.

2242.correction: A demonstration shows that it works for that one specific case. A proof allows us to know all cases that are true.

7543.statement: Pupils may struggle to write a correct opposing statement.
7543.correction: Encourage pupils to discuss the various proposed opposing statements presented in the first learning cycle. What does each statement actually mean?

5878.belief: Proofs have to be solely algebraic and do not involve diagrams.
5878.statement: Proofs have to be solely algebraic and do not involve diagrams.
5878.correction: Proofs involve showing that a conjecture holds for multiple cases (general case). A diagram can represent multiple cases.

7487.statement: Pupils may struggle with showing why the false proofs are false.
7487.correction: Checking what each variable represents will help pupils see why each of the 'proofs' do not work.

9305.belief: Since there is no common difference, further terms in the sequence cannot be generated.
9305.statement: Since there is no common difference, further terms in the sequence cannot be generated.
9305.correction: Pupils have seen sequences where the first difference is not common and seen examples of other rules. In this lesson, the concept of a second difference is introduced and this can be used to generate the next first difference.

9306.belief: Since there is no common difference, it is impossible to find the n^th term.
9306.statement: Since there is no common difference, it is impossible to find the n^th term.
9306.correction: The first learning cycle shows how we can build quadratic sequences from n^2 and a linear sequence.

8338.belief: $$u_1$$ means that $$u$$ has a value of one.
8338.statement: Pupils may think that $$u_1$$ means that $$u$$ has a value of one.
8338.correction: $$u_1$$ refers to the first term in the sequence and $$u_2$$ refers to the second term. The subscript refers to the term number.

6745.statement: Pupils get confused between simple interest and compound interest. When presented with a compound interest problem the common error is for pupils to add the same constant amount.
6745.correction: Visual representations are helpful here. The bar models in the first part of the lesson show how compound interest grows year on year. The graphical representation also demonstrates the fundamental difference between the two forms of interest.

6437.statement: Pupils are very familiar with exponents but the introduction of 'subscript' notation may confuse them. For example, they may think $$x_2$$ must be a function of $$x$$ because $$x^2$$ is.
6437.correction: Use of language helps. When talking through an iterative formula like $$x_{t+1}=8x_t +6$$ say, "The next $$x$$ value is equal to eight lots of the current $$x$$ value plus six" whilst pointing at it. Get pupils to do the same back to you.

8623.statement: Some pupils want to clear their calculator display and type every single level of iteration in each time.
8623.correction: Encourage the pupils to trust their 'Ans' button. Get them to work on an example whereby they physically type the input value in and type the whole formula again. Then get them to repeat the same question using the 'Ans' button. Time this if you can!

3001.belief: To find a solution to a given degree of accuracy an iteration can just be rounded.
3001.statement: To find a solution to a given degree of accuracy an iteration can just be rounded.
3001.correction: Several successive iterations need to round to the same value to a given degree of accuracy. If in doubt efficient calculator use means many iterations can be generated easily until confident that a digit is fixed.

918.belief: A change in sign always indicates a solution. No change in sign means no solution.
918.statement: A change in sign always indicates a solution. No change in sign means no solution.
918.correction: A change in sign only indicates a solution if the equation is equal to zero and if the graph of the equation crosses the $$x$$ axis between those points. Where there is a repeated root or two solutions between them there may be no change in sign.

3888.belief: An iterative formula can always be used to find the solutions to an equation.
3888.statement: An iterative formula can always be used to find the solutions to an equation.
3888.correction: This lesson addresses limitations of iteration. Some formulas will cause an error becasue we are unable to evaluate the square root of a negative or divide by 0. Other formulas may not converge. Different values of $$x_0$$ produce different results.

5606.belief: Plotting the midpoint of the class against the cumulative frequency.
5606.statement: Plotting the midpoint of the class against the cumulative frequency.
5606.correction: Ensure that the pupils are clear that each cumulative frequency includes all values up to the upper boundary of each group.

10700.belief: Using the highest value on the y-axis rather than the total frequency when calculating the values to read off for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile.
10700.statement: Using the highest value on the y-axis rather than the total frequency when calculating the values to read off for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile.
10700.correction: Ensure pupils understand that the total frequency must be used. A graph where the y-axis goes up to 100 and the total frequency is 40 can be used to highlight this. Then repeat with the same data, but with a graph where the y-axis goes up to 200.

3101.belief: Forgetting to order the list of data before finding the 5 key pieces of information.
3101.statement: Forgetting to order the list of data before finding the 5 key pieces of information.
3101.correction: Ask some pupils to stand at the front of the classroom. Find the person in the middle, and pose the question "is they the median sized person?" Repeat with quartiles. This should highlight the importance of putting the numbers in order first.

8822.belief: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
8822.statement: Not referring to the context of the question when comparing the data.
8822.correction: Highlight that just saying the median or the interquartile is bigger is of little use unless you know what the data was about.

3494.belief: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
3494.statement: Histograms with unequal bar widths are plotted against the frequency and/or pupils read the frequency density as the frequency of the class width.
3494.correction: Show what a histogram with unequal bar widths looks like when plotted against frequency. This visual aid will show pupils the distribution of data is difficult to see.

10694.belief: When using Desmos, incorrect brackets () are used to input raw data as elements.
10694.statement: When using Desmos, incorrect brackets () are used to input raw data as elements.
10694.correction: [] are used to denote a set of data elements or elements. Encourage pupils to think about set notation when using Venn diagrams. Desmos will reject the use of () as they do not denote a set of elements.

7318.statement: Pupils may struggle to combine inequalities.
7318.correction: Encourage pupils to use a number line and draw on the potential solutions. In order for a solution set to be valid for all the stated inequalities, it must include values that satisfy all potential solution restrictions.

28.belief: 3 > x > 9 is a valid way to combine x < 3 and x > 9.
28.statement: 3 > x > 9 is a valid way to combine x < 3 and x > 9
28.correction: Test a value to show pupils that this does not make sense. When x = 0, it is true that x < 3 but not true that x > 9 so 3 > 0 > 9 does not work.

10304.belief: X = 4 is a line parallel to the x axis and that y = 4 is parallel to the y axis.
10304.statement: Thinking that x = 4 is a line parallel to the x axis and that y = 4 is parallel to the y axis.
10304.correction: Consider the points along the line. Writing valid coordinate pairs lets pupils identify which coordinate stays the same and which one changes.

3772.belief: All inequalities are graphed with solid lines.
3772.statement: All inequalities are graphed with solid lines.
3772.correction: When graphed, strict inequalities are indicated with a dashed line. This is important as it visually tells us that values on the line will not satisfy the inequality.

6759.statement: Pupils may give an angle rather than a bearing.
6759.correction: Remind pupils that a bearing is an angle, measured clockwise from North and given as three figures.

1784.belief: A common error is to not substitute into all variable terms where there is more than one in a function. For example, 'Write a simplified expression for f$$(x+3)$$ when f$$(x)=x^2-4x$$'.
1784.statement: A common error is to not substitute into all variable terms where there is more than one in a function. For example, 'Write a simplified expression for f$$(x+3)$$ when f$$(x)=x^2-4x$$'
1784.correction: Use brackets when substituting. For example, for 'Write a simplified expression for f$$(x+3)$$ when f$$(x)=x^2-4x$$' you would write f$$(x+3)=(x+3)^2-4(x+3)$$

7239.statement: Pupils may not see the vertical translation depending on the function used to show the effect of $$a$$.
7239.correction: Ensure pupils consider a range of functions so that they can see the movement of the graph.

2881.belief: F$$(x)+5$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$y$$-direction so pupils may assume that f$$(x+5)$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$x$$-direction.
2881.statement: f$$(x)+5$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$y$$-direction so pupils may assume that f$$(x+5)$$ is a translation of $$+5$$ in the $$x$$-direction.
2881.correction: Visually showing pupils, using graphing technology, that f$$(x+5)$$ is not a translation to the right will help. Showing them a comparison of the two tables of values for both functions shows them why this happens.

6738.statement: Pupils can get confused between $$-$$f$$(x)$$ and f$$(-x)$$, which one is a reflection in the $$x$$-axis and which is a reflection in the $$y$$-axis?
6738.correction: Interpreting the notation is key. Remind pupils that $$-$$f$$(x)$$ is the output of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$-1$$. Which coordinate is the output? The $$y$$ coordinates are altered from positive to negative, that is a reflection in which axis?

6987.statement: Pupils mix-up $$-$$f$$(x)$$ and f$$(-x)$$. Which is a reflection in the $$x$$-axis? Which is in the $$y$$-axis?
6987.correction: f$$(-x)$$ is the input being multiplied by $$-1$$ before the function is applied. Which coordinate is the input? The $$x$$ coordinates change from positive to negative so this must be a reflection in the $$y$$ axis.

6272.statement: Pupils confuse 'stretch' transformations. Many transformations of the form $$y=a$$f$$(x)$$ have the appearance of a compression towards the $$y$$-axis rather than a 'stretch' in the $$y$$-direction.
6272.correction: Interpreting the notation is key. $$y=a$$f$$(x)$$ is the output of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$a$$. Which coordinate is the output? The $$y$$ coordinates change by a scale factor of $$a$$ so this must be a stretch in the $$y$$-direction.

6273.statement: Pupils confuse 'stretch' transformations. Does the transformation $$y=$$f$$(ax)$$ affect the $$x$$ or $$y$$ coordinates?
6273.correction: Interpreting the notation is key. $$y=$$f$$(ax)$$ is the input of f$$(x)$$ being multiplied by $$a$$. Which coordinate is the input?

1771.belief: For the combined transformation $$3$$f$$(x-2)$$ order does not matter so pupils may assume that order never matters.
1771.statement: For the combined transformation $$3$$f$$(x-2)$$ order does not matter so pupils may assume that order never matters.
1771.correction: For $$3$$f$$(x-2)$$ the $$3$$ affects the output, the $$y$$ value, and the $$-2$$ affects the input, the $$x$$ value. Model to show that these can happen in either order. Then point out that $$3$$f$$(x)-2$$ is two effects on the output.

7228.statement: Pupils may not see the link between transformations and manipulating algebraic expressions.
7228.correction: Be explicit in highlighting that the graph of $$y=x^2+10x+22$$ is the graph of $$y=(x+5)^2-3$$ which is the graph of $$y=x^2$$ transformed by the translation, "$$5$$ units left, $$3$$ units down".
